The assignment drops the global's reference, `GC.gc()` frees the 800 MB, and the last expression shows live MB so you can confirm. If live bytes do not fall, something else refers to the array (another global, a closure, a captured view, a cache). Use `julia_get_session_variables` to see what is left. A function-local temporary needs none of this: write `f() = sum(rand(10^8))` and call it.
How do I check that a command-line tool exists before running it?

Use `Sys.which`, which returns the path or `nothing`:

```julia
tool = Sys.which("sort")
isnothing(tool) && error("required tool `sort` was not found on PATH")
readchomp(pipeline(`printf 'b\na\n'`, `sort`))
```

Fail fast with a message naming the missing tool, instead of letting `run` raise a less specific error later. When the tool is a hard requirement of a package, document it, and check its `--version` output if you depend on particular behavior.
Why does it matter which Julia version `juliac` uses when I have several installed?

The verifier and the patched Base live in that Julia, so verdicts are only valid for it. The app launcher records its Julia at install time: `juliac --version` can print `julia version 1.12.7` while the shell's default `julia` is 1.13.2, as it did for juliac 0.3.8 before the app was reinstalled (it then printed `juliac version 0.3.12, julia version 1.13.2`). If you test code with 1.13 and ship a binary built by 1.12 (or the reverse), a construct could pass in one and fail in the other. Make them agree: reinstall the app under the Julia you ship with, and record `juliac --version` in the build log.
Returning `nothing` from a function feels like returning `null` in Java: the caller can forget to check and get a crash somewhere far away.

The failure mode is different, and the difference is the point.

A Java `null` has the static type of the thing it stands in for, so it can travel through code typed `String` and only fails when something dereferences it, possibly far from where it was produced. Julia's `nothing` has type `Nothing`, which is not a subtype of anything you would otherwise accept. The first operation that was not written for it fails right there:

```julia
x = findfirst(==(7), [1, 2, 3])    # nothing
try
    x + 1
catch e
    println(first(split(sprint(showerror, e), '\n')))
end
```

```text
MethodError: no method matching +(::Nothing, ::Int64)
```

That is a `MethodError` at the use site, not a crash three modules later. And unlike `null`, it is visible to the type system: `Base.return_types(f, ...)` shows `Union{Nothing, T}`, so a static analysis tool, or just reading `@code_warntype`, tells you exactly which values can be absent, and a function with a `::T` return annotation refuses `nothing` at construction time.

What can still bite:

- Storing the value in an `Any`-typed container, which hides the union again. Keep containers concretely typed (`Vector{Union{Nothing,T}}`).
- Code paths with no operation on the value at all, e.g. passing it straight to `println`, which happily prints `nothing`. If absence must be an error there, use `something(x)`, which throws if given only `nothing`.

So the discipline is the same as with any sum type: branch on it (`isnothing`) or unwrap it (`something`) at the first use. The language makes forgetting loud instead of silent.
how to check a functions return type at repl

`typeof(f(x))` for the actual value. `Base.return_types(f, (Int,))` and `@code_warntype f(1)` show what the compiler infers. For ordinary work `typeof` is enough.

```julia
f(x) = x > 0 ? 1 : 1.0
(typeof(f(1)), typeof(f(-1)), Base.return_types(f, (Int,))) # → (Int64, Float64, Any[Union{Float64, Int64}])
```

An inferred `Union{Float64, Int64}` means the return type depends on a runtime value: sometimes fine, sometimes a performance hint.
`@ccall toupper('a'::Char)::Cint` returns a huge number instead of 65. How do I pass characters?

A Julia `Char` is a 32-bit value holding the UTF-8 bytes in the high end, not a code point. Declaring the argument `::Char` passes that raw encoding (`0x61000000` for `'a'`), which C reads as `int`. Convert to the C type first:

```julia
wrong = @ccall toupper('a'::Char)::Cint        # → 1627389952
right = @ccall toupper(Cint('a')::Cint)::Cint  # → 65
(wrong, Char(right))
```

C `char` is `Cchar` (a signed byte on most platforms), not `Char`. For text, pass `Cstring`/`Ptr{UInt8}`; for single code points use `Cint(c)`, or `Cwchar_t(c)` for `wchar_t` APIs. `Char(code)` converts a C code point back, and `Char(UInt8(code))` converts a byte, assuming Latin-1.
How do I count how many elements satisfy a condition, or get the position of the max?

```julia
v = [3, 8, 1, 8]
(count(>(2), v), argmax(v), argmin(v), findall(==(maximum(v)), v)) # → (3, 2, 3, [2, 4])
```

`argmax` returns the first position of a maximum. Using `sum(v .> 2)` also counts, but allocates a Boolean array; `count(>(2), v)` doesn't.
writting a varargs macro @names_values a b c that prints a = 1, b = 2 ... for any number of vars

A macro can take `args...`; each element is an expression you can stringify and splice.

```julia
macro names_values(vars...)
    stmts = [:(println($(string(v)), " = ", $(esc(v)))) for v in vars]
    return Expr(:block, stmts...)
end

a, b, c = 1, "two", 3.0
@names_values a b c
@names_values
```

Output:

```text
a = 1
b = two
c = 3.0
```

With no arguments the macro returns an empty `block`, which evaluates to `nothing`. Each variable is escaped so it is looked up in the caller; the `string(v)` label is built at expansion time.
Is there a way to make the test run stop at the first failing item instead of running all 300 of them?

Pass `failfast=true`:

```julia
using TestItemRunner
@run_package_tests failfast=true
```

The run stops after the first item that fails or errors, and the remaining items are not run at all, so they appear in neither the summary nor the counts. I confirmed that the items after a deliberately failing one were missing from the summary. Use it for a quick red/green check; use a normal run when you need the complete list of failures.
How do I make an unavoidable abstract-typed call static for an enumerable set of types?

Enumerate with `isa` checks and call a concrete method in each branch ("manual union splitting"):

```julia
abstract type Shape end
struct Circle <: Shape; r::Float64; end
struct Square <: Shape; s::Float64; end
area(c::Circle) = pi * c.r^2
area(s::Square) = s.s^2

function area_any(x::Shape)
    x isa Circle && return area(x)
    x isa Square && return area(x)
    throw(ArgumentError("unsupported shape"))
end
println(Base.return_types(area_any, (Shape,)))
println(area_any(Square(2.0)))
```

This prints `Any[Float64]` and `4.0`. The explicit ladder fails fast on a type you did not list, instead of a dynamic dispatch. Prefer a `Union{Circle,Square}` or a tagged struct when the set is closed.
What is the difference between `export` and `public`? When should I use each?

`export name` makes `name` available after `using Module` and also marks it public. `public name` (Julia 1.11 and later) declares `name` part of the module's documented API without exporting it, so users call it qualified (`Module.name`) and `using` does not bring it into scope.

```julia
module Pubt
export a
public b
a() = 1
b() = 2
c() = 3
end

println(Base.ispublic(Pubt, :a), " ", Base.ispublic(Pubt, :b), " ", Base.ispublic(Pubt, :c))
using .Pubt
println(isdefined(@__MODULE__, :a), " ", isdefined(@__MODULE__, :b))
println(Pubt.b())
```

Output:

```text
true true false
true false
2
```

Use `export` sparingly for the few names users want unqualified; use `public` for supported API that would be too generic to export, like helpers and extension points. `public` has no effect on name resolution, only on the API contract and on docs and tooling. Code that must also load on Julia before 1.11 cannot use the `public` keyword directly, because older parsers reject it.
My array wrapper loses its type after `v .+ 1`: I get a `Vector`. How do I make broadcasting return my type?

By default a broadcast over an `AbstractArray` subtype uses `DefaultArrayStyle`, which allocates an `Array`. Give your type its own style and tell Base how to allocate output with `similar(bc, ElType)`.

```julia
struct MyVec{T} <: AbstractVector{T}
    data::Vector{T}
end
Base.size(v::MyVec) = size(v.data)
Base.getindex(v::MyVec, i::Int) = v.data[i]
Base.setindex!(v::MyVec, x, i::Int) = (v.data[i] = x)
Base.similar(v::MyVec, ::Type{T}, dims::Dims) where {T} = MyVec(Vector{T}(undef, dims...))

v = MyVec([1, 2, 3])
before = typeof(v .+ 1)

Base.BroadcastStyle(::Type{<:MyVec}) = Broadcast.ArrayStyle{MyVec}()
Base.similar(bc::Broadcast.Broadcasted{Broadcast.ArrayStyle{MyVec}}, ::Type{T}) where {T} =
    MyVec(Vector{T}(undef, length(axes(bc)[1])))

w = MyVec([0, 0, 0])
w .= v .* 2
(before, typeof(v .+ 1), typeof(sin.(v)), typeof(v .+ (1:3)), w)
```

The result is `(Vector{Int64}, MyVec{Int64}, MyVec{Float64}, MyVec{Int64}, [2, 4, 6])`. `map` already returned a `MyVec` before the style existed, because it goes through `similar(v, T, dims)`. Broadcasting uses a separate path, so it needs the style and the `similar(bc, ...)` method.
make an autotuned/benchmarked knob (block size, crossover length) trim safe

Do not measure at run time inside the code you trim. Measure offline, store the result as a preference, and read it into a `const`:

```julia
using Preferences

const BLOCK = @load_preference("block", 64)::Int      # compile-time constant

function process!(y::AbstractVector, x::AbstractVector)
    for i in eachindex(y, x)
        y[i] = 2x[i]
    end
    return y
end
```

`@load_preference` runs when the module is precompiled, so `BLOCK` is a plain constant in the image: overridable by the user, never detected live, and identical in the verified build and the shipped binary. An unpinned runtime autotune result is a value of unknown type or origin, and in a trimmed library it is a common source of unresolved calls. Changing a preference invalidates precompilation, so remember to rebuild.
How do I use Preferences.jl to let users choose a backend for my package?

Declare `Preferences` as a dependency of your package, read the value at load time, and let users set it with `set_preferences!`, which writes `LocalPreferences.toml` in the active project.

```julia
# src/MyPkg.jl
module MyPkg
using Preferences
const BACKEND = @load_preference("backend", "default")
backend() = BACKEND
end
```

```julia
using Preferences, MyPkg
set_preferences!(MyPkg, "backend" => "fast"; force=true)
```

I ran this: the first process printed `default`, the file then contained `[MyPkg]` / `backend = "fast"`, and a fresh process printed `fast`. A preference read into a `const` at load time is part of the compiled cache, so a change takes effect in a new session, not in the running one.
Why do you put `Pkg.activate(".")` before `Pkg.add`, if I started Julia in the project directory?

Starting Julia in a directory does not activate its project. Only `--project` (or `JULIA_PROJECT`, or `Pkg.activate`) does; otherwise the default global environment is active. Verify, rather than assume:

```julia
Base.active_project()
```

If the printed path ends in `environments/v1.xx/Project.toml`, you are in the global environment and a `Pkg.add` would put the package there. This check costs nothing and prevents modifying the wrong environment, so make it a habit before any `Pkg.add`, `Pkg.rm`, `Pkg.compat` or `Pkg.develop`.
My CI is green on Julia 1.13 but red on 1.10. I only have 1.13 locally.
Install the LTS (`juliaup add 1.10`) and reproduce there before changing code. From the agent tools, call `julia_run_testitems` with `julia_cmd` set to the 1.10 `julia` binary and `max_workers=1`.
On 1.10 an item fails with a `BoundsError` inside an `@inbounds` loop.

That fits the version difference: on 1.10 `Pkg.test()` forces `--check-bounds=yes`, which neutralizes `@inbounds` and exposes the bad index, while a default 1.13 `Pkg.test()` inherits the session setting and hides it. Fix the indexing (iterate `eachindex`, or establish the in-bounds property and cover it with a test). Then on 1.13 run `Pkg.test(; julia_args=["--check-bounds=yes"])` so local runs match CI.
write macro @unroll i 1:3 body that expands to 3 copies of body with i = 1, 2, 3

Require a literal `a:b` range, so the macro can compute the iteration values at expansion time without calling `eval`. Each copy gets its own `let` binding.

```julia
macro unroll(i, range, body)
    Meta.isexpr(range, :call, 3) && range.args[1] === :(:) &&
        range.args[2] isa Integer && range.args[3] isa Integer ||
        error("@unroll needs a literal integer range a:b, got: $range")
    stmts = [:(let $(esc(i)) = $k
                  $(esc(body))
              end) for k in range.args[2]:range.args[3]]
    return Expr(:block, stmts...)
end

@unroll i 1:3 println("i = ", i)

f() = @unroll k 1:4 (k^2)
println(f())
println(try @macroexpand(@unroll i 1:n println(i)) catch e; e.msg end)
```

Output:

```text
i = 1
i = 2
i = 3
16
@unroll needs a literal integer range a:b, got: 1:n
```

The block returns the value of its last copy. Unrolling duplicates code, so it pays off only for small fixed counts in hot code, and it is something to benchmark rather than assume: the compiler already unrolls many short loops.
I just fixed a bug in `parse_header` in `src/parser.jl`. How should I verify it?

Run the parser's items, not the whole suite:

```text
1. julia_list_testitems       name_pattern="parse"           # get the ids
2. julia_run_testitems        name_pattern="parse"  max_workers=1
3. julia_get_testitem_detail  testrun_id=<id>  testitem_ids=[<failed ids>]   # only on failure
```

If the bug had no failing test, add one and confirm it fails against the old code before you rely on it. Run the full suite only if `parse_header` is shared by other components, as a gate before the commit.
Can I seed with `Random.seed!(1)` in a test and compare to hard-coded numbers from the output?

I call `eval` on my macro's argument so the macro can "run it". It fails for local variables. Why?

```julia
macro run(ex)
    eval(ex)
end
function f()
    v = 3
    @run v + 1
end
```

Macros run at expansion time, before any variable has a value, and `eval` there uses the macro's module, so `v` is not found (and defining `f` itself fails). A macro should *return* the expression, to be compiled where the macro is called.

```julia
macro run(ex)
    esc(ex)
end

function f()
    v = 3
    @run v + 1
end
println(f())
```

Output:

```text
4
```

Rule: a macro that calls `eval` on its arguments is almost always wrong. Return code; do not run it.
"setting x = nothing frees memory immediately" - right or wrong

No. `x = nothing` only removes one reference. The object is freed when the garbage collector next runs and finds it unreachable, and only if nothing else references it (another variable, a closure, a view of it, a container, a cache). To free it now and confirm:

```julia
x = zeros(10^7)
GC.gc(); with_x = Base.gc_live_bytes()
x = nothing
GC.gc(); without_x = Base.gc_live_bytes()
with_x - without_x > 70_000_000
```

Then there is a second layer: even when Julia has freed memory, process RSS may or may not drop, depending on the allocator. Use `Base.gc_live_bytes()` to know whether Julia still holds the data.
many io bound operations, how to limit concurrency, also does the result order stay the same

`asyncmap(f, xs; ntasks = n)` runs `f` over `xs` with at most `n` tasks active and returns results in input order. It uses `@async`-style tasks, so it suits waiting on I/O, not CPU-bound work.

```julia
active = Ref(0)
peak = Ref(0)
function fetch_one(i)
    active[] += 1
    peak[] = max(peak[], active[])
    sleep(0.01)                 # stands in for a network call
    active[] -= 1
    return i * 2
end

out = asyncmap(fetch_one, 1:20; ntasks = 4)
println(out == (1:20) .* 2)
println(peak[] <= 4)
```

The counters are safe here because `asyncmap` tasks share a thread and switch only at `sleep`. For CPU-bound work use chunked `Threads.@spawn`, or `Threads.foreach` over a channel.
Where does `LOAD_PATH` come from and what do `@`, `@v#.#` and `@stdlib` mean?

```julia
Base.load_path()   # the expanded stack of environments
```

The default `LOAD_PATH` is `["@", "@v#.#", "@stdlib"]`:

- `@` is the active project (`--project` or `Pkg.activate`).
- `@v#.#` is the default global environment for this Julia version (for example `v1.13`) in the first depot.
- `@stdlib` is the standard library that ships with the Julia installation.

`using Foo` searches these in order, and the first environment that provides `Foo` wins. You can override the whole stack with the `JULIA_LOAD_PATH` environment variable.
What is the difference between `Threads.nthreads()` and `Threads.maxthreadid()`, and which do I use to size per-thread storage?

`Threads.nthreads()` counts threads in the default pool (`nthreads(:interactive)` the interactive ones). `Threads.maxthreadid()` is, per its docstring, "a lower bound on the number of threads (across all thread pools)" and is at least any `threadid()` you have observed. Thread ids from different pools share one id space, so `nthreads()` is not a safe array size for `threadid()`-indexed storage.

```julia
println(Threads.nthreads(:default), " ", Threads.nthreads(:interactive))
println(Threads.maxthreadid() >= Threads.nthreads(:default) + Threads.nthreads(:interactive))
println(Threads.threadid() <= Threads.maxthreadid())
```

Better: do not index by `threadid()` at all. A task can migrate between threads at any yield point, so per-task state (`Base.OncePerTask`, or a buffer created inside each spawned task) is the correct unit.
How do I make a `Pair` and what is `=>` for?

`a => b` creates a `Pair`. It's what `Dict` is built from, and what iterating a dictionary yields. Pairs also appear in `replace`, `sort` options, and `DataFrame`-style APIs.

```julia
p = "x" => 1
(p.first, p.second, first(p), last(p), Dict(["a" => 1, "b" => 2])) # → ("x", 1, "x", 1, Dict("a" => 1, "b" => 2))
```
Pythagorean triples with perimeter at most p

```julia
function pythagorean_triples(p::Integer)
    p >= 0 || throw(ArgumentError("p must be non-negative"))
    out = Tuple{Int,Int,Int}[]
    for a in 1:p÷3, b in a:p÷2
        c2 = a^2 + b^2
        c = isqrt(c2)
        c * c == c2 && a + b + c <= p && push!(out, (a, b, c))
    end
    return out
end

# Checks
@assert pythagorean_triples(12) == [(3, 4, 5)]
@assert pythagorean_triples(30) == [(3, 4, 5), (5, 12, 13), (6, 8, 10)]
@assert pythagorean_triples(5) == []
@assert all(t -> t[1]^2 + t[2]^2 == t[3]^2, pythagorean_triples(200))
```

`isqrt` gives an exact integer square root, so the test `c*c == c2` is free of floating-point error. Since a <= b < c, the loops can be bounded by p/3 and p/2. The search is O(p^2); Euclid's formula would generate primitive triples directly.
[compat] Reexport = "1.2.2" pins to exactly 1.2.2, true?

No. A bare version is a caret range: `"1.2.2"` allows any `1.x.y` that is at least `1.2.2` and below `2.0.0`. `Pkg.add` writes that form (it wrote `"1.2.2"` for Reexport on Julia 1.11 and later), which is why you often want to loosen the lower bound to the oldest release you actually support (`"1.2"` or even `"1"`).

Exact pinning is written `"=1.2.2"`. Pinning a library's own dependency exactly makes it hard to install alongside other packages, so reserve it for emergencies.
How do I find out which registered versions of a package exist?

In a session, the registry in your depot is the source of truth. It has one directory per package with a `Versions.toml` file listing each registered version and its tree hash, for example `registries/General/R/Reexport/Versions.toml` under the first depot (the file exists in my depot). Reading it needs no network.

Pkg tells you indirectly as well: a failing request lists them, as in `possible versions are: 0.2.0 - 1.2.2 or uninstalled` when I asked for Reexport 99.0. If you only want to know whether an update is available for something you use, `Pkg.status(outdated=true)` is simpler.
I wrote solve(prob, Tsit5(), rtol=1e-6) and got an error. What's wrong?

The keyword is `reltol`, not `rtol`. Misspelled solver options are rejected with "Unrecognized keyword arguments found.":

```julia
using OrdinaryDiffEqTsit5

decay!(du, u, p, t) = (du[1] = -p.k * u[1]; nothing)
prob = ODEProblem(decay!, [1.0], (0.0, 5.0), (k = 1.0,))
sol = solve(prob, Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-6, abstol = 1e-8)
```

Absolute tolerance matters when a state passes near zero, since a purely relative criterion cannot be met there; set both.
How do I compare floating point results in tests?

Use `isapprox` (`≈`) with a tolerance chosen for the algorithm. Exact `==` on computed floats is a latent failure.

```julia
using Test
@test 0.1 + 0.2 ≈ 0.3
println(0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3)   # false
@test isapprox(0.1 + 0.2, 0.3; atol=1e-12)
```

`≈` uses a relative tolerance by default, which is useless near zero: comparing against `0.0` needs an explicit `atol`. Use `==` only where exactness is the contract (integers, a bit-exact reference).

Write `second_largest(v)` returning the second largest distinct value, and throwing an `ArgumentError` if there are fewer than two distinct values. Reply with a single ```julia code block containing the complete code.

```julia
function second_largest(v)
    u = sort!(unique(v); rev = true)
    length(u) >= 2 || throw(ArgumentError("need at least two distinct values"))
    return u[2]
end
```
How do I use `on` to react to a click or a change, and later remove the callback?

`on` registers a function on an Observable and returns a handle; `off(handle)` unregisters it.

```julia
using CairoMakie

a = Observable(1.0)
handle = on(a) do v
    println("a = ", v)
end

a[] = 6.0     # prints "a = 6.0"
off(handle)
a[] = 7.0     # nothing printed
```

In an interactive backend, `events(fig).mousebutton`, `events(fig).keyboardbutton`, and `Button(...).clicks` are Observables, so `on(btn.clicks) do _ ... end` handles button clicks. Callbacks that update plots run on the main task; keep them short, and do slow work elsewhere, then write the result to an Observable.
turn "12x" or "" into numbers without crashing

Use `tryparse` when bad input is expected; use `parse` when it is a bug and you want the exception.

```julia
tryparse(Int, "12x")        # → nothing
tryparse(Float64, "")       # → nothing
parse(Float64, "1e3")       # → 1000.0
parse(Int, "ff"; base=16)   # → 255
parse(Int, " 12 ")          # → 12
parse(Int, "12x")           # → ArgumentError: invalid base 10 digit 'x' in "12x"
```

`parse` and `tryparse` allow surrounding whitespace. `tryparse` never throws on malformed numeric text, so branch on `nothing`:

```julia
function read_int(s, default)
    v = tryparse(Int, s)
    return something(v, default)
end
read_int("7", 0), read_int("seven", 0)  # → (7, 0)
```

For `Union{T,Nothing}` results from `tryparse`, `something(v, default)` is more direct than an `if`.
Why does `Some` exist? `Some(x)` just seems like a box around `x`.

It exists to distinguish "no value" from "a value that happens to be `nothing`". With a bare `Union{Nothing,T}` those collapse into the same thing.

```julia
cfg = Dict{String,Any}("timeout" => nothing)   # key present, value nothing
get(cfg, "timeout", :absent)                   # nothing  -- indistinguishable from...
get(cfg, "retries", :absent)                   # :absent
```

A lookup that returns `Some(value)` or `nothing` keeps the two apart:

```julia
cfg = Dict{String,Any}("timeout" => nothing)
lookup(d, k) = haskey(d, k) ? Some(d[k]) : nothing
lookup(cfg, "timeout"), lookup(cfg, "retries")
```

```text
(Some(nothing), nothing)
```

`something` unwraps `Some` and skips `nothing`, so the two compose:

```julia
something(Some(nothing), 1)   # nothing  -- a present value, even though it is nothing
something(nothing, 1)         # 1        -- absent, so the default
```

Where this matters in practice:

- Dictionaries and configuration where `nothing` is a legitimate stored value.
- Keyword arguments whose default means "not given" when `nothing` is also a valid explicit setting: `f(; x=nothing)` cannot tell them apart, `f(; x=Some(nothing))` can, though usually a different sentinel reads better.
- Generic containers (`Union{Nothing, Some{T}}` for an optional slot whose `T` might itself be `Nothing`).

Everywhere else, plain `Union{Nothing,T}` is simpler and is what Base uses. Do not wrap return values in `Some` by default; reach for it only when `nothing` is a possible *value*.

Review this path handling:

```julia
config = home * "/.config/" * app * "/settings.toml"
parts = split(config, "/")
sep = Sys.iswindows() ? ";" : ":"
dirs = split(ENV["PATH"], sep)
```

Three problems. Hand-built separators break on Windows (`\`), `split(path, "/")` breaks on Windows paths, and `ENV["PATH"]` raises `KeyError` if unset. Use the path functions, which work on every platform:

```julia
home = homedir()
app = "demo"
config = joinpath(home, ".config", app, "settings.toml")
parts = splitpath(config)
name = basename(config)
dir = dirname(config)

pathsep = Sys.iswindows() ? ';' : ':'
dirs = split(get(ENV, "PATH", ""), pathsep; keepempty = false)

(name, parts[end-1], eltype(dirs) <: AbstractString)
# → ("settings.toml", "demo", true)
```

`joinpath`, `splitpath`, `basename`, `dirname`, `splitext`, `normpath`, and `abspath` handle separators and edge cases such as trailing slashes. The separator between entries of `PATH` is `;` on Windows and `:` elsewhere. For well-known locations use `homedir()`, `tempdir()`, `mktempdir()`, `Sys.BINDIR`, or `DEPOT_PATH` instead of literals such as `/tmp` or `~`.
How do I get the right Julia type for a C `bool` argument or flags field?

For C99 `bool` / `_Bool` (one byte, 0 or 1), `Bool` is correct as an argument, a return type, and a struct field. For an `int` used as a flag, use `Cint` and convert explicitly; for `unsigned char` flags use `Cuchar`.

```c
int is_even(int x);          // returns 0 or 1 here, but other libraries return any nonzero value
```

```julia
const libdemo = "./libdemo"

is_even(x::Integer) = (@ccall libdemo.is_even(x::Cint)::Cint) != 0
(is_even(4), is_even(7))     # → (true, false)
```

Write the comparison on the Julia side (`!= 0`) rather than trusting the C function to return exactly 1. Passing a Julia `Bool` to a `Cint` parameter works (`true` converts to `1`); returning one from an `int` declaration is the bug.
How do I make a plot depend on a slider?

Build the plotted data from `slider.value` with `lift`. The slider's `value` is an `Observable`, so the plot redraws as it moves (in an interactive backend like GLMakie):

```julia
using CairoMakie

xs = range(0, 2π, 200)
fig = Figure()
ax = Axis(fig[1, 1])
sl = Slider(fig[2, 1], range = 0:0.1:2π, startvalue = 1)
ys = lift(s -> sin.(s .* xs), sl.value)
lines!(ax, xs, ys)

set_close_to!(sl, 2.0)           # move programmatically
sl.value[]                       # → 2.0
save("slider.png", fig)          # a static snapshot works with CairoMakie
```

In a headless session, you can still drive the observables by assignment and save snapshots, which is also how to test interactive code. Keep expensive computation out of the `lift` function, or it runs on every slider tick.
Is `uppercase(::Char)` OK in a trimmed program? Someone told me Unicode tables are a trim problem.

Treat that as a hypothesis for your toolchain, not a rule. In a test build with `juliac` 0.3.12 on Julia 1.13.2 (and earlier with juliac 0.3.8 on 1.12.7), this program built clean and printed `A` for an input starting with `a`:

```julia
function (@main)(args::Vector{String})::Cint
    c = uppercase(first(args[1]))
    println(Core.stdout, c)
    return 0
end
```

A scan that checks against stock `Base` can still flag `uppercase(::Char)` because the Unicode category lookup is not allocation-free or trim-clean in every Julia version. If your domain is ASCII, comparing bytes yourself avoids the question and the table entirely:

```julia
upper_ascii(c::Char) = 'a' <= c <= 'z' ? Char(UInt8(c) - 0x20) : c
println(upper_ascii('q'), upper_ascii('Q'), upper_ascii('1'))
```

This prints `QQ1`. Verify with the real build for the Julia version you ship before rewriting working code.
Fail early with a clear message if an external tool isnt installed.

Resolve the program with `Sys.which` before the first use. It searches `PATH` the way the OS would and returns the full path or `nothing`. Throw a message that names the tool and how to get it, instead of letting an `IOError: could not spawn` surface later.

```julia
function require_tool(name::AbstractString)
    path = Sys.which(name)
    path === nothing && error("required program `$name` was not found on PATH; install it or add it to PATH")
    return path
end

sh = require_tool("sh")
(basename(sh), Sys.which("no_such_program_xyz"))
# → ("sh", nothing)
```

Interpolate the resolved path into the command (`` `$sh -c ...` ``) so the same binary is used throughout. Check once at package load, in a setup function, or at the entry point of the feature that needs the tool, not deep in a loop. If a JLL provides the program, use that (`Zstd_jll.zstd()`), and you need no check at all.
Is `s[1:3]` safe to use on arbitrary text to take the first 3 characters?

No. A range indexes bytes, and both endpoints must be character starts (the end may be any index that starts a character; the slice includes that whole character). On non-ASCII text it can throw:

```julia
s = "héllo"
s[1:2]  # → "hé"
s[1:3]  # → StringIndexError: invalid index [3], valid nearby indices [2]=>'é', [4]=>'l'
```

Use `first` and `last`, which count characters:

```julia
s = "héllo"
first(s, 3)  # → "hél"
last(s, 3)   # → "llo"
```

For an arbitrary character range, convert endpoints with `nextind`: `s[nextind(s, 0, 2):nextind(s, 0, 4)]`.

Why does `sort!` return the array if it mutates? Do I need to assign the result?

It returns the (same) mutated array purely for convenience, so you can chain. You don't need to assign it, and assigning gives a second name for the same array, not a copy.

```julia
v = [3, 1, 2]
w = sort!(v)
(w === v, v) # → (true, [1, 2, 3])
```

A common bug is `v = push!(v, 4)` (harmless) versus `v = sort(v)` (fine) versus expecting `sort(v)` alone to change `v` (it does not).
How do I silence a noisy function I call, or turn off all logging temporarily?

Scope the silence to the call with `NullLogger`:

```julia
using Logging
noisy() = (@info "chatter"; @warn "more chatter"; 42)
value = with_logger(NullLogger()) do
    noisy()
end
value
```

`with_logger` returns the value of the block, and the logger applies to everything the block calls, including tasks it starts. For a process-wide switch use `Logging.disable_logging(level)`, which disables all messages at that level and below. It *returns the new level*, and you restore with `disable_logging(Logging.BelowMinLevel)`:

```julia
using Logging
old = disable_logging(Logging.Warn)    # Debug, Info and Warn are now off
@error "still shown"
disable_logging(Logging.BelowMinLevel) # everything on again
```

Silencing hides diagnostics, so keep it narrow. If a library warns about something real, fix the cause rather than muting it.
Can I pass a `view` or a `SubArray` of a vector to `ccall` as a pointer?

Only when the elements are contiguous, and Julia will not stop you when they are not. Conversion to a pointer succeeds for a strided view and yields the address of the first element, so C then walks consecutive memory instead of the selected elements:

```julia
x = collect(1.0:6.0)
s = view(x, 1:2:5)                 # elements 1.0, 3.0, 5.0
p = Base.unsafe_convert(Ptr{Float64}, s)
seen = GC.@preserve x unsafe_wrap(Array, p, 3)   # what C would read
(collect(s), seen, strides(s))
```

A contiguous range (`view(x, 3:5)`) is fine: the pointer is that of `x[3]`. Check `strides(v) == (1,)` (or use `Base.iscontiguous`) before passing a view, or pass `collect(s)` (a fresh contiguous `Vector`) and copy results back if C writes to it. In a public function, either convert with `Vector{Float64}(a)` or restrict the annotation to `DenseVector`.
what else is && and || for apart from booleans, also does it short circuit

They short-circuit, so they double as compact control flow: `cond && action` runs `action` only if `cond` is true; `cond || action` runs it only if `cond` is false. Common for guards and early exits.

```julia
function first_big(v)
    isempty(v) && return nothing
    v[1] > 100 || return "small"
    return "big"
end

(first_big([]), first_big([5]), first_big([500])) # → (nothing, "small", "big")
```

The `a & b` and `a | b` operators are the non-short-circuit versions (broadcast them as `(x .> 0) .& (y .> 0)`). Use `&&`/`||` for scalars. Don't write `if x > 0 && y` when `y` is not a `Bool`; the last operand's value is the result.
My test fails intermittently. How do I debug something that doesn't reproduce every time?

Make it deterministic first, then shrink it.

1. **Fix the random seed.** Random numbers are the most common source. Seed at the start of the test:

```julia
using Random
Random.seed!(1234)
a = rand(3)
Random.seed!(1234)
a == rand(3)
```

With the same seed you get the same numbers. When a failure appears at some seed, print the seed in the test name or message so it can be replayed.

2. **Check for concurrency.** `Threads.nthreads()` and tasks writing shared state without a lock give results that vary with scheduling. Run with `JULIA_NUM_THREADS=1` (or `julia -t 1`): if the failure disappears, you have a data race to find.
3. **Check for order and environment dependence**: tests that share global state, depend on the working directory or on `Dict` iteration order of mixed keys.
4. **Loop it.** Run the failing item many times in one session: `for i in 1:1000; f() || (println("failed at ", i); break); end`.
5. **Use `rtol`.** Floating-point results that differ in the last bits across machines or thread counts (summation order) belong to `isapprox`, not `==`.

Capture the failing inputs (log them or store them in a global) so you can re-run exactly that case.

I need to use `Serialization` (a standard library) in my package. Stdlib UUIDs are fixed and I can see it in Julia's own Project.toml, so I'll add the line to `[deps]` directly and save the round trip.

Use `Pkg.add("Serialization")` anyway. The UUID may well be correct, but a hand edit skips the manifest update and any compat handling, and it leaves the other environments (the `test/` project, a `docs/` project) inconsistent until you remember to resolve each one. `Pkg.add` is one call:

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.activate(".")
Pkg.add("Serialization")
```

Then review the `[compat]` line it may write: on Julia 1.11 and later it records the standard-library version of the Julia you ran (for example `"1.11.0"`), which excludes Julia 1.10's `Serialization`. Relax it with `Pkg.compat("Serialization", "1")` if you support 1.10.
Why do the tools report durations in milliseconds in one place and seconds in another?

Inputs and outputs use different units: `timeout` and `max_wait_seconds` are in seconds, while every duration in a result is in milliseconds (per item, the time that item took; in the summary, elapsed wall-clock time for the whole run). Convert before comparing a `timeout=8` setting against a result showing `duration: 8321`.
Chairmarks or BenchmarkTools? What are the practical differences?

Both give trustworthy statistics when used properly. Chairmarks needs no tuning phase, so sweeps over many configurations take seconds; BenchmarkTools is the long-standing default and many tutorials use it.

```julia
using Chairmarks, Statistics

x = rand(1000)
@b sum($x)                         # one summary sample
b = @be sum($x) seconds = 0.1      # a set of samples
length(b.samples) > 1              # → true
median(b).time < 1e-3              # → true: .time is in SECONDS
fieldnames(typeof(first(b.samples)))
# → (:evals, :time, :allocs, :bytes, :gc_fraction, :compile_fraction, :recompile_fraction, :warmup)
```

Things to remember:

- Chairmarks' `.time` is in seconds, BenchmarkTools' in nanoseconds. A units mistake when switching harnesses is easy to make.
- The default time budget (`seconds`) is short. A call that takes ~50 ms yields only one or two samples. Check `length(b.samples)`; a single sample prints with `median == min`.
- Stateful or mutating targets need the setup phase: `@be setup f(_)`. Benchmarking `update!(ws); solve!(ws)` directly measures re-solving the same problem.
- Samples record `gc_fraction` and `compile_fraction`, which tells you whether a slow sample was GC or compilation.

Pick one per project and use it consistently, so numbers in the repository are comparable.
Axis(fig[1,1], xlable="t") did not complain when I wrote it in a notebook cell but the label is missing.

A typo in an `Axis` attribute should throw immediately; in current Makie it does:

```julia
using CairoMakie
Axis(Figure()[1, 1], xlable = "t")
# ERROR: Invalid attribute xlable for block type Axis.
```

If you saw no error, the misspelling was probably passed to a plot function instead (plots collect extra keywords as attributes), or the cell output was swallowed. The correct keyword is `xlabel`. You can also set attributes after creation, which fails the same way if misspelled:

```julia
using CairoMakie
ax = Axis(Figure()[1, 1])
ax.xlabel = "t (s)"
ax.title = "decay"
```

List valid attributes with `?Axis` in the REPL.
Coin change: minimum number of coins to make an amount, or nothing if impossible

```julia
function min_coins(coins::AbstractVector{<:Integer}, amount::Integer)
    amount >= 0 || throw(ArgumentError("amount must be non-negative"))
    all(>(0), coins) || throw(ArgumentError("coin values must be positive"))
    INF = typemax(Int)
    best = fill(INF, amount + 1)
    best[1] = 0
    for a in 1:amount, c in coins
        if c <= a && best[a-c+1] != INF
            best[a+1] = min(best[a+1], best[a-c+1] + 1)
        end
    end
    return best[end] == INF ? nothing : best[end]
end

# Checks
@assert min_coins([1, 2, 5], 11) == 3
@assert min_coins([25, 10, 1], 30) == 3
@assert min_coins([5, 3], 7) === nothing
@assert try min_coins([0, 1], 5); false catch e; e isa ArgumentError end
```

`best[a+1]` is the fewest coins for amount `a`; each amount extends a smaller reachable amount by one coin. The `INF` sentinel is checked before adding one so it never overflows. Time is O(amount x #coins). Greedy would fail on coin sets like `[25, 10, 1]` for some amounts, which is why DP is used.
My symmetric matrix gives complex eigenvalues from `eigen(A)`. Why, and what should I do?

Plain `eigen(A)` first tests whether `A` is exactly symmetric. If so it uses the symmetric solver (real, ascending eigenvalues). If `A` is symmetric only up to rounding or noise, the test fails, the general nonsymmetric algorithm runs, and close eigenvalues can come back as a complex pair. Wrap in `Symmetric` (or `Hermitian`) when the asymmetry is noise; the solver then reads one triangle.

```julia
using LinearAlgebra
A = [1.0 1e-8; -1e-8 1.0]          # double eigenvalue plus tiny asymmetric noise
(issymmetric(A), eltype(eigen(A).values), eltype(eigen(Symmetric(A)).values), eigvals(Symmetric(A)))
```

```text
(false, ComplexF64, Float64, [0.9999999900000001, 1.00000001])
```

`Symmetric(A)` silently discards the lower triangle, so use it only when you know the asymmetry is noise; otherwise find the source of it. `(A + A') / 2` is the explicit symmetrization. For just a few eigenvalues, `eigvals(Symmetric(A), 1:3)` computes only the lowest three.
Two of my own measurements of the same function disagree. How do I debug?

Suspect the environment before the code. Checklist:

1. Same Julia version and thread count? `VERSION`, `Threads.nthreads()`.
2. `BLAS.get_num_threads()` identical in both?
3. Other Julia processes running (`ps -eo pid,etime,rss,args | grep '[j]ulia'`)?
4. Was the session reused? A leftover method definition or global can change which code runs: `which(f, Tuple{...})`.
5. Was each timing warmed up and taken as a median?

Record these values next to every result. Only after they match should you look at the code.
my custom logger never prints but @info works with the default one

Check, in order:

1. **Minimum level.** `ConsoleLogger(io)` and `SimpleLogger(io)` default to `Info`, so `@debug` is filtered. Pass the level: `ConsoleLogger(io, Logging.Debug)`.
2. **Is it installed?** Constructing a logger does nothing; use `with_logger(logger) do ... end` or `global_logger(logger)`. Confirm with `Logging.current_logger()`.
3. **Buffering.** A logger writing to a file or `IOBuffer` shows nothing until you flush/close the file or read the buffer. A `SimpleLogger` file was empty until flush in my test.
4. **Global disable.** `Logging.disable_logging(level)` earlier in the session turns messages off for every logger; undo with `disable_logging(Logging.BelowMinLevel)`.
5. **Wrong stream.** Logs go to `stderr`; a tool that captures only `stdout` misses them, though the MCP evaluator returns both in its output.

```julia
using Logging
lg = ConsoleLogger(stdout, Logging.Debug)
with_logger(lg) do
    (typeof(Logging.current_logger()), Logging.min_enabled_level(Logging.current_logger()))
end
```

```julia
x = rand(10^6)
s = 0.0
for i in eachindex(x)
    s += x[i]
end
```
top level loop takes forever, same code in a function is fast. why

At top level, `x` and `s` are global variables, so the compiler cannot assume their types and every iteration boxes and dispatches dynamically. In a script file (not the REPL) the loop also fails to see `s` as the global without `global s`, because of soft-scope rules. Put the work in a function:

```julia
function total(x)
    s = zero(eltype(x))
    for i in eachindex(x)
        s += x[i]
    end
    s
end

x = rand(10^6)
total(x)
@allocated total(x)        # → 0
```

I measured the top-level version (with `global s += x[i]` so that it runs in a file) allocating about 100 MB for a million iterations, and running more than a hundred times slower than the function. The rule: only put setup and calls at top level; put every loop in a function and pass data as arguments. This is the single most common cause of "Julia is slow" reports.

Why does `@sprintf("%.0f", 2.5)` give "2" and not "3"?

The conversion is exact and ties round to even, like C's `printf`. `2.5` is exactly representable, so it is a true tie and goes to the even neighbor. `round` has the same tie rule by default; request the other behavior explicitly.

```julia
using Printf

(@sprintf("%.0f", 2.5), @sprintf("%.0f", 3.5), @sprintf("%.1f", 0.25),
 round(2.5), round(3.5), round(2.5, RoundNearestTiesAway), round(1.2345, RoundUp; digits=2))
```

The result is `("2", "4", "0.2", 2.0, 4.0, 3.0, 1.24)`. Numbers like `0.15` are not exactly representable in binary, so their formatted result depends on the stored value, not on the decimal text you typed.
are random numbers reproducable when I use threads or `@spawn`

Yes, as long as the task structure is deterministic. The default RNG is `TaskLocalRNG`: each task has its own state, seeded when the task is created from its parent's state (without advancing the parent's). So the same seed and the same spawn order gives the same numbers regardless of scheduling. Sharing a single non-task-local RNG object across tasks is not safe and gives non-reproducible results.

```julia
using Random

f() = (Random.seed!(1); fetch(Threads.@spawn rand()))
same_child = f() == f()

work(rng) = sum(rand(rng, 1000))
rngs = [Xoshiro(i) for i in 1:2]
par = fetch.([Threads.@spawn work(rng) for rng in rngs])
seq = [work(Xoshiro(i)) for i in 1:2]
(same_child, par == seq, typeof(Random.default_rng()))
```

The result is `(true, true, Random.TaskLocalRNG)`. Giving each task its own `Xoshiro(i)` (one per work item, seeded from the item's index) is the simplest way to make parallel results independent of how many threads run.
Do invalidations mean I wrote a bug?

No. An invalidation is a consequence of adding a more specific method that code compiled earlier could have called. It makes the earlier compiled code stale and it is recompiled, correct but slow. Invalidations from your own definitions are routine; they hurt when a package's methods invalidate lots of compiled code in packages it merely depends on, adding to everyone's latency. SnoopCompile's `invalidation_trees` shows which method caused which invalidations, and the usual fix is to make the offending method signature less broad or add a type annotation at the call site.

Review my `iterate`. It loops forever on `for x in Take3(...)`.

```julia
struct Take3
    v::Vector{Int}
end
Base.iterate(t::Take3) = (t.v[1], 1)
Base.iterate(t::Take3, i) = i >= 3 ? nothing : (t.v[i+1], i)
```

The state never advances: the second method returns `i` instead of `i + 1`, so it yields `t.v[i+1]` forever until the guard `i >= 3`, which is never reached. The state must be what you need to produce the next element. Also guard the first call against an empty vector.

```julia
struct Take3
    v::Vector{Int}
end

function Base.iterate(t::Take3, i=1)
    (i > 3 || i > length(t.v)) && return nothing
    return (t.v[i], i + 1)
end
Base.length(t::Take3) = min(3, length(t.v))
Base.eltype(::Type{Take3}) = Int

(collect(Take3([10, 20, 30, 40])), collect(Take3([1])), collect(Take3(Int[])))
```

The result is `([10, 20, 30], [1], Int64[])`. Using `eachindex(t.v)` or delegating to `Iterators.take(t.v, 3)` is simpler if you do not need a custom type at all.
Why is my mutable struct slow compared to an immutable one? Should I use `mutable struct` by default?

No: default to `struct`. Immutable structs of plain-data fields can live on the stack or inline in arrays; a `mutable struct` is heap-allocated and referenced by pointer. Use `mutable struct` only when identity and in-place update matter (a counter, a cache, an iterator state).

To update an immutable struct "in place", create a modified copy:

```julia
struct Pt
    x::Int
    y::Int
end

p = Pt(1, 2)
q = Pt(p.x + 1, p.y)
(p, q) # → (Pt(1, 2), Pt(2, 2))
```

Packages like Accessors.jl provide `@set` for deep functional updates.
Should I shell out to `tar` and `curl` in my package, or use something in Julia?

Prefer the standard libraries when they cover the job. They work on every platform, need no external program on `PATH`, and raise ordinary Julia exceptions: `Tar` for tar archives, `Downloads` for HTTP(S) and FTP, `SHA` for checksums, `Base64`, `LibGit2` for git operations, `Dates`, `Sockets`.

```julia
using Tar

dir = mktempdir()
mkpath(joinpath(dir, "src"))
write(joinpath(dir, "src", "a.txt"), "x")

tarball = joinpath(dir, "src.tar")
Tar.create(joinpath(dir, "src"), tarball)
Tar.extract(tarball, joinpath(dir, "out"))
(readdir(joinpath(dir, "out")), length(Tar.list(tarball)))
# → (["a.txt"], 1)
```

Order of preference for a capability: (1) Julia's standard library or a registered Julia package; (2) a `*_jll` library via `ccall`; (3) a `*_jll` executable run as a subprocess; (4) a system program found with `Sys.which`, with an explicit availability check. Each step down adds portability risk and process-startup cost.
What does `Ref` do?

`Ref(x)` is a mutable one-element container. Read and write with `r[]`. Use it where you want a mutable cell: a counter shared by a closure, a `const` global that changes, or a scalar passed by reference.

```julia
function make_counter()
    count = Ref(0)
    return () -> (count[] += 1)
end

next = make_counter()
(next(), next(), next()) # → (1, 2, 3)
```

In `broadcast`, `Ref(x)` tells Julia to treat `x` as a scalar: `in.(1:3, Ref([2, 3]))`.
Which is better, `sum(f.(v))` or `sum(f, v)`? They look equivalent.

`sum(f, v)` applies `f` while reducing and allocates nothing; `sum(f.(v))` materializes `f.(v)` as a full array first:

```julia
f_fused(v) = sum(abs2, v)
f_temp(v)  = sum(abs2.(v))
v = rand(1000)
f_fused(v); f_temp(v)
@allocated(f_fused(v)), @allocated(f_temp(v))
```

```text
(0, 8072)
```

Same answer, one extra 8 KB array per call for the broadcast version. In a hot loop that is a GC cost for nothing.

The pattern generalizes: `maximum(f, v)`, `minimum(f, v)`, `any(f, v)`, `all(f, v)`, `count(f, v)`, `mapreduce(f, op, v)`, `sum(f, v; init)`. Each takes the function as the first argument and fuses the map into the reduction. `mapreduce(f, op, v; init=x)` is the general form, and `sum(f, v)` is `mapreduce(f, +, v)` with pairwise summation for accuracy.

Where the broadcast form is right: when you need the mapped array for something else as well, or when `f` broadcasts over several arrays (`sum(a .* b)`, which has no `sum(f, a, b)` form; write `sum(prod, zip(a, b))` or `mapreduce(*, +, a, b)` instead, or use `dot`).

`sum(f(x) for x in v)` is a third option and also allocates nothing, but `sum(f, v)` is shorter and dispatches to specialized reductions for ranges and arrays.

Column normalization on a big image stack is slow; profiling points to this loop:

```julia
function normalize_cols!(A::AbstractMatrix, s::AbstractVector)
    for i in axes(A, 1), j in axes(A, 2)
        A[i, j] /= s[j]
    end
    return A
end
```

Julia arrays are column-major: `A[i, j]` and `A[i+1, j]` are adjacent in memory, while `A[i, j]` and `A[i, j+1]` are a whole column apart. In `for i, for j` the inner loop varies `j`, so every access jumps a column ahead and uses a new cache line. Make the first index the innermost loop:

```julia
function normalize_cols!(A::AbstractMatrix, s::AbstractVector)
    axes(A, 2) == axes(s, 1) || throw(DimensionMismatch("one scale per column required"))
    for j in axes(A, 2)
        sj = s[j]
        for i in axes(A, 1)
            A[i, j] /= sj
        end
    end
    return A
end

A = [1.0 2.0; 3.0 4.0]
normalize_cols!(A, [1.0, 2.0])  # → [1.0 1.0; 3.0 2.0]
```

Both orders compute the same values; only the memory access pattern differs. To measure it on your data:

```julia
using BenchmarkTools
function normalize_cols_rowwise!(A, s)
    for i in axes(A, 1), j in axes(A, 2)
        A[i, j] /= s[j]
    end
    return A
end

A = rand(4000, 4000); s = rand(4000) .+ 1
@btime normalize_cols_rowwise!($A, $s)
@btime normalize_cols!($A, $s)
```

Which parts of this are anti-patterns for performance? Quick review.

```julia
using LinearAlgebra
results = []
function run_all(data)
    for d in data
        r = d' * d
        push!(results, r)
    end
end
```

Two problems. `results = []` is a non-constant global of type `Vector{Any}`, so every `push!` and every later read is untyped. And the loop pushes into a global from inside the function. Return the result, with a concrete element type:

```julia
using LinearAlgebra

function run_all(data)
    results = Float64[]
    sizehint!(results, length(data))
    for d in data
        push!(results, d' * d)
    end
    return results
end

data = [rand(10) for _ in 1:100]
r = run_all(data)
r isa Vector{Float64}                   # → true
Base.return_types(run_all, (typeof(data),))    # → Any[Vector{Float64}]
```

Also note `d' * d` for a real vector is the dot product, and `dot(d, d)` or `sum(abs2, d)` states it directly without the adjoint wrapper. If `data` can contain different numeric types, derive the element type from the data instead of hard-coding `Float64`: `Vector{eltype(eltype(data))}()`.

What's the right way to build a lookup of results for many inputs in a loop without growing a Dict?

```julia
function squares_dict(keys_)
    d = Dict{Int,Int}()
    for k in keys_
        d[k] = k^2
    end
    d
end
```

If you know the number of entries, tell the Dict, so it does not rehash while growing. If keys are dense integers, use a vector instead, which has no hashing at all:

```julia
function squares_dict(ks)
    d = Dict{Int,Int}()
    sizehint!(d, length(ks))
    for k in ks
        d[k] = k^2
    end
    d
end

function squares_vec(n)
    out = Vector{Int}(undef, n)
    for k in 1:n
        out[k] = k^2
    end
    out
end

ks = 1:1000
squares_dict(ks); squares_vec(1000)
squares_dict(ks)[10] == squares_vec(1000)[10]   # → true
```

`Dict{Int,Int}()` with explicit key and value types avoids boxing (a `Dict()` is `Dict{Any,Any}`). Use a dictionary when the keys are sparse or non-integer, and a vector indexed by key when they are small dense integers. Measure the two at your size before restructuring the data.
How do I build a DataFrame row by row in a loop?

Either collect the data into vectors (or a vector of named tuples) and build the frame once, or start from a typed empty frame and `push!`.

```julia

rows = [(a = i, b = i^2) for i in 1:3]
DataFrame(rows)
```

```text
3×2 DataFrame
 Row │ a      b
     │ Int64  Int64
─────┼──────────────
   1 │     1      1
   2 │     2      4
   3 │     3      9
```

```julia
using DataFrames
df = DataFrame(a = Int[], b = Int[])     # typed columns
for i in 1:3
    push!(df, (i, i^2))
end
nrow(df)  # → 3
```

Do not grow a frame with `df = vcat(df, newrow)` in a loop: each call copies every column, so the loop is quadratic.

My `julia_eval_code` call returned `status: "error"`. Did the tool break?

No. A Julia exception inside your code comes back as a normal result with `status: "error"`, carrying the message and backtrace. The value, captured output, and error status are separate fields. Read the message and stack trace, fix the code or the source, and call `julia_eval_code` again in the same session. Do not kill the session over an exception; the process is still alive and still warm.
why --check-bounds=yes for the pre-merge test gate

`--check-bounds=yes` makes every `@inbounds` annotation inert, so an out-of-range index in code marked `@inbounds` raises `BoundsError` instead of silently reading or writing arbitrary memory. The gate is the one place where an unjustified `@inbounds` has to show up as a failure. In my run, a function with `@inbounds v[1]` on an empty vector raised `BoundsError` under `check_bounds = 1` and returned a value without any error under `check_bounds = 0`, so a test using `@test_throws BoundsError` passed in one mode and failed in the other.

Practical consequence: if a package uses `@inbounds`, its tests need to run at least once under `--check-bounds=yes`, either through plain `Pkg.test()` on Julia 1.10-1.12 (which force it) or, on 1.13 and later (where `Pkg.test()` inherits the session's setting), by passing `julia_args=["--check-bounds=yes"]` explicitly. In CI, `julia-actions/julia-runtest` takes `check_bounds: 'yes'`; state it explicitly rather than relying on its default.

My XOR scrambler isn't reversible. Running it twice with the same key doesn't give back the original file.

```julia
function xor_stream(out::IO, in::IO, key::UInt8)
    while !eof(in)
        write(out, Char(read(in, UInt8) ⊻ key))
    end
end
```

XOR with a key often produces a byte of `0x80` or more, and `write(out, Char(...))` turns each of those into a two-byte UTF-8 sequence. The second pass then XORs those extra bytes too, so the original is not recovered:

```julia
src = UInt8[0x48, 0x65, 0x6c, 0x6c, 0x6f]
once = IOBuffer()
xor_stream(once, IOBuffer(src), 0xff)
length(take!(once))  # → 10
```

Write the `UInt8` directly:

```julia
function xor_stream(out::IO, in::IO, key::UInt8)
    while !eof(in)
        write(out, read(in, UInt8) ⊻ key)
    end
    return out
end

src = UInt8[0x48, 0x65, 0x6c, 0x6c, 0x6f]
once = IOBuffer()
xor_stream(once, IOBuffer(src), 0xff)
twice = IOBuffer()
xor_stream(twice, IOBuffer(take!(once)), 0xff)
take!(twice) == src  # → true
```

The type of the value you hand to `write` decides what is written, so make sure it is a `UInt8` and not a `Char` or an `Int` (an `Int` writes eight bytes).
My audit script says "no findings" but I know the function allocates. What could be wrong?

Check that the checks were actually enabled before believing the result. With checks switched off, every assertion expands to the bare call and the audit passes vacuously, with output identical to a clean run. In StrictMode, `checks_enabled()` reports the state and `assert_enabled()` returns `true` when checks are on. Put it first in the script:

```julia
using StrictMode
assert_enabled()
fs = StrictMode.audit(MyPkg; format = :json)
```

The state is baked in at precompile time, so changing the preference needs a fresh session. The principle holds beyond this package: before reporting that a checker passed, confirm that it ran and that it can fail.

How do I use workgroup-local memory and `@synchronize`?

Allocate a tile with `@localmem T dims`, have each work item fill its slot, call `@synchronize` (a barrier across the workgroup), then read slots written by other work items. Every work item in the group must reach the same `@synchronize`, so keep it outside divergent branches.

```julia
using KernelAbstractions

@kernel function group_sum!(out, @Const(inp))
    gi = @index(Group, Linear)
    li = @index(Local, Linear)
    i  = @index(Global, Linear)
    tile = @localmem eltype(inp) (4,)      # one slot per work item of a size-4 group
    tile[li] = inp[i]
    @synchronize
    if li == 1
        s = zero(eltype(inp))
        for k in 1:4
            s += tile[k]
        end
        out[gi] = s
    end
end

inp = Float32.(1:8)
out = zeros(Float32, 2)
group_sum!(CPU(), 4)(out, inp; ndrange = 8)
println(out)
```

Output: `Float32[10.0, 26.0]`. The tile size must match the workgroup size you launch with (4 here). For ordinary sums, call `sum(x)` on the array instead of writing this by hand.

Two of my sessions and four test workers are alive and I just need to finish one more small edit. How should I handle memory?

Keep the session you are using (killing it costs a recompile), and free the rest if the machine is tight:

1. `julia_list_sessions` and `julia_list_test_processes` to see everything.
2. `julia_terminate_test_process` for idle workers you will not need now (they restart on demand with a startup cost).
3. `julia_kill_session` for extra sessions that you created and no longer use.
4. For the final check, `julia_run_testitems` with `items=[...]` and `max_workers=1`.

After the task is complete, kill the sessions you created and terminate the workers. Sessions or workers created by other agents or the user are not yours to kill.
Why is running `julia -e 'using MyPkg; check()'` after every edit so slow even when the package is already precompiled?

Compile cost is paid per process start, not per edit. Every `julia -e` launch starts a fresh runtime, loads the package, and compiles every specialization `check()` needs from scratch, even with a warm precompile cache (which only stores what the package's own precompile workload covered). Edit count does not matter; process count does.

Fix: keep one persistent process and send each check to it. With the JuliaMCP tools:

```text
1. julia_create_session  (project=/path/to/MyPkg, package=/path/to/MyPkg, package_name="MyPkg")
2. julia_eval_code       (session_id=..., code="using MyPkg; check()")
3. edit src/..., then julia_eval_code again with the same session_id
```

The first eval pays the compile cost; later evals reuse compiled code and Revise recompiles only what you changed. A check that takes tens of seconds cold typically takes well under a second warm, so there is no reason to batch or skip checks.
I need to left-pad numbers with zeros and format floats. `lpad`? `@sprintf`?

```julia
using Printf
lpad(7, 3, '0')                  # → "007"
rpad("ab", 5, '.')               # → "ab..."
@sprintf("%5.2f|%-5d|%05d", 3.14159, 42, 42)  # → " 3.14|42   |00042"
@sprintf("%x", 255)              # → "ff"
@sprintf("%+d", 5)               # → "+5"
@sprintf("%8.3e", 1234.5)        # → "1.234e+03"
```

`lpad`/`rpad` take any value that `string` accepts (`lpad(7, 3, '0')` works on an integer). `@sprintf` takes a literal format string known at parse time. For a format held in a variable use `Printf.Format` and `Printf.format`:

```julia
using Printf
fmt = Printf.Format("%d items")
Printf.format(fmt, 3)  # → "3 items"
```

Build the `Format` once outside a loop if you reuse it. Padding with `lpad` is by character count, while `@sprintf("%5s", ...)` pads by character count too; neither accounts for display width of East Asian characters (see `textwidth`).
How do I get unique elements, counts, and find indices?

```julia
v = [3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3]
(unique(v), count(==(3), v), findall(==(3), v), findfirst(==(2), v), findlast(==(1), v)) # → ([3, 1, 2], 3, [1, 3, 6], 4, 5)
```

`findfirst`/`findlast` return `nothing` if nothing matches, `findall` returns an empty vector. For frequency counts use a `Dict`:

```julia
v = [3, 1, 3, 2, 1, 3]
counts = Dict{Int,Int}()
for x in v
    counts[x] = get(counts, x, 0) + 1
end
sort(collect(counts)) # → 3-element Vector{Pair{Int64, Int64}}:
#    1 => 2
#    2 => 1
#    3 => 3
```

Write `parse_duration("1d2h3m4s")` returning whole seconds as an Int. Units must be d, h, m, s in that order, each at most once. Reject everything else (empty string, wrong order, stray text, non-ASCII digits, trailing newline, numbers that overflow) with errors that quote the input.

```julia
const DURATION = r"\A(?:([0-9]+)d)?(?:([0-9]+)h)?(?:([0-9]+)m)?(?:([0-9]+)s)?\z"

function parse_duration(s::AbstractString)
    m = match(DURATION, s)
    (m === nothing || all(isnothing, m.captures)) &&
        throw(ArgumentError("invalid duration \"$s\"; expected units d, h, m, s in that order, e.g. \"1h30m\""))
    secs = 0
    for (cap, unit) in zip(m.captures, (86400, 3600, 60, 1))
        cap === nothing && continue
        n = tryparse(Int, cap)
        n === nothing && throw(ArgumentError("number too large in duration \"$s\""))
        secs = Base.checked_add(secs, Base.checked_mul(n, unit))
    end
    return secs
end

# Checks
@assert parse_duration("1h30m") == 5400
@assert parse_duration("1d2h3m4s") === 93784

for bad in ("", "1m1h", "5ñ", "٣s", " 1h", "1h\n", "1h1h", "h", "1.5h", "12")
    err = try parse_duration(bad); nothing catch e; e end
    @assert err isa ArgumentError && occursin("invalid duration", err.msg) && occursin(bad, err.msg)
end
@assert (try parse_duration("9223372036854775807d"); false catch e; e isa OverflowError end)
```

The regex is anchored with `\A` and `\z`; `^` and `$` would let `"1h\n"` through because `$` also matches before a final newline. Digits are spelled `[0-9]` because `\d` can match Unicode digits that `tryparse(Int, ...)` then rejects. Optional groups give `nothing` captures for absent units, and the all-`nothing` case (the empty string) is rejected explicitly. Parsing uses `tryparse` so an out-of-range number becomes an `ArgumentError`, while the final sum uses `checked_add` and `checked_mul` so overflow raises `OverflowError` instead of wrapping.
I would like to add a feature that creates a ZIP archive, but I do not want the users to have to install anything. Could you tell me what I should use? Many thanks in advance.

Use the 7-Zip build that ships with Julia, `p7zip_jll`. Its `p7zip()` function returns a `Cmd` for a binary that is present on every Julia installation. Interpolate it and pass arguments as separate words:

```julia
using p7zip_jll

function make_zip(archive::AbstractString, files::AbstractVector{<:AbstractString})
    isfile(archive) && rm(archive)                     # `7z a` would add to an existing archive
    run(pipeline(`$(p7zip_jll.p7zip()) a -tzip -bso0 -bsp0 $archive $files`))
    return archive
end

function extract_zip(archive::AbstractString, dest::AbstractString)
    run(pipeline(`$(p7zip_jll.p7zip()) x -bso0 -bsp0 -o$dest $archive`; stdout = devnull))
    return dest
end

dir = mktempdir()
a, b = joinpath(dir, "a.txt"), joinpath(dir, "b.txt")
write(a, "hello archive\n"); write(b, "second\n")
archive = make_zip(joinpath(dir, "out.zip"), [a, b])
out = extract_zip(archive, joinpath(dir, "x"))
(sort(readdir(out)), read(joinpath(out, "a.txt"), String))
# → (["a.txt", "b.txt"], "hello archive\n")
```

`-bso0 -bsp0` silence 7-Zip's output and progress streams; `-o` takes its directory with **no space** after it (`-o$dest` is one argument). For tar archives use the `Tar` standard library, and for downloads `Downloads.download`: both are pure Julia and need no subprocess at all.

My loop has `@inbounds` and returns weird numbers instead of an error. How do I find the bad index?

```julia
function s(v)
    t = 0
    for i in 1:4
        @inbounds t += v[i]
    end
    t
end
```
Called with a 3-element vector, `s([1,2,3])` printed `139972215386582`.

`@inbounds` told the compiler to skip the check, so `v[4]` read whatever memory sits after the array. Run the script with checks forced on; this neutralizes every `@inbounds`:

```text

```

which turns the silent garbage into

```text
ERROR: LoadError: BoundsError: attempt to access 3-element Vector{Int64} at index [4]
Stacktrace:
 ...
 [4] s(v::Vector{Int64})
   @ Main /tmp/jl_hcwD5Z/ib.jl:4
```

The fix is in the loop range. Iterate over the array's own indices, which also removes the need for the annotation:

```julia
function s(v)
    t = zero(eltype(v))
    for i in eachindex(v)
        t += v[i]
    end
    t
end
s([1, 2, 3])
```

On Julia 1.12 and earlier `Pkg.test()` runs the test process with `--check-bounds=yes`; on 1.13 it does not force it, so call `Pkg.test(; julia_args = ["--check-bounds=yes"])`. For ad hoc runs, pass the flag to `julia`. Measure before putting `@inbounds` back: for a loop like this the check is often already eliminated.
My numeric CSV column came back as `String`. Why?

CSV.jl infers a column type from the values it sees. One non-numeric token (`NA`, `-`, `N/A`, a stray `x`) makes the whole column text unless you tell it that token means missing.

```julia
using CSV, DataFrames
txt = "id,score\n1,3.5\n2,NA\n3,4\n"
eltype(CSV.read(IOBuffer(txt), DataFrame).score)                          # → String3
eltype(CSV.read(IOBuffer(txt), DataFrame; missingstring = "NA").score)    # → Union{Missing, Float64}
```

Then check the result: `eltype.(eachcol(df))` and `describe(df)`.

Forcing `types=Float64` on a column with a bad token does not stop at the error by default: CSV.jl logs a warning and stores `missing`. To fail fast, pass `strict = true`:

```julia
using CSV, DataFrames
txt = "a\n1.5\n2.5\nx\n"
err = try
    CSV.read(IOBuffer(txt), DataFrame; types = Float64, strict = true)
catch e
    e
end
typeof(err)  # → CSV.Error
```
What does `memory_threshold` do on `julia_run_testitems`?

It recycles a worker whose resident memory grows too large. Per the tool schema: after each test item finishes, if the worker's own resident memory exceeds this fraction of total system memory, the worker is replaced and its remaining items are redistributed (no result is lost). It is off by default. The fraction is of total memory, so on a 64 GB machine `0.02` is about 1.3 GB per worker.

```text
julia_run_testitems  max_workers=2  memory_threshold=0.03  timeout=300
```

Use it for suites whose workers keep growing run after run (large fixtures, caches, globals pinning arrays). It does not bound memory within a single item; a single item that needs more than the machine has will still be killed. Fix growth at its source when you can (do not keep large test data in globals; set it to `nothing` and call `GC.gc()` at the end of the item).

Does a variable like `e` in my macro's `catch e` clash with a user variable named `e`?

```julia
macro catch_error(ex)
    quote
        try
            $(esc(ex)); nothing
        catch e
            e
        end
    end
end
e = "user e"
r = @catch_error (println(e); error("boom"))
```

No. Hygiene renames the macro's `e`, so the user expression still sees its own `e`.

```julia
macro catch_error(ex)
    quote
        try
            $(esc(ex)); nothing
        catch e
            e
        end
    end
end
e = "user e"
r = @catch_error (println(e); error("boom"))
println(r)
println(e)
```

Output:

```text
user e
ErrorException("boom")
user e
```

The user's `println(e)` printed the user's string, the macro returned the exception it caught, and the user's `e` is unchanged. If the macro had escaped the whole quote, `catch e` would have overwritten the user's variable.

how to close a library opened with `dlopen` and when would I need to

Call `Libdl.dlclose(handle)` when you are done. In most packages you never need to: libraries stay loaded for the life of the process, and closing one while any pointer into it (function pointers from `dlsym`, `@cfunction` pointers handed to the library, data it allocated with its own allocator) is still in use is undefined behavior. It matters for plugins loaded on demand and for tests that rebuild a library.

```julia
using Libdl

h = Libdl.dlopen("./libdemo")
f = Libdl.dlsym(h, :point_size)
size_before = @ccall $f()::Csize_t
path_ok = basename(Libdl.dlpath(h)) == "libdemo.so"    # dlpath maps a handle back to its file
Libdl.dlclose(h)
(size_before, path_ok)       # → (0x0000000000000018, true)
```

After `dlclose`, `f` is dangling. Do not call it. Note that rebuilding a library file while the same path is still loaded in the process does not update the loaded copy: the old version stays mapped until it is unloaded (and may remain if something else holds it), so recompile to a new file name or restart the session when testing changes.
Pkg.status shows ⌃ ⌅ ⚲ and [yanked], what do they mean

From the `Pkg.status` documentation:

- `⌃` a newer version is available and installable, for example with `Pkg.update`.
- `⌅` a newer version exists but cannot be installed because of compatibility constraints; `Pkg.status(outdated=true)` shows which.
- `⚲` the package is pinned (`Pkg.pin`), which I saw in the output after pinning Reexport.
- `[yanked]` the installed version has been withdrawn from the registry, for example for a bug or vulnerability; update or replace it.

Run `Pkg.status(mode=Pkg.PKGMODE_MANIFEST)` to see the same for indirect dependencies.
does Pkg.add write a [compat] entry for me automaticaly

It depends on the Julia version and on the kind of project. I checked adding Reexport to a package project (one with `name` and `uuid`) and to a plain environment:

| Julia | package project | plain environment |
|---|---|---|
| 1.10 | no `[compat]` entry | no entry |
| 1.11, 1.12, 1.13 | `Reexport = "1.2.2"` | no entry |

So never assume it; open `Project.toml` after every add and look. `julia` itself never gets an entry from `Pkg.add`. Set it yourself:

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.compat("julia", "1.10")
```

The auto-written bound is the version that happened to resolve (`"1.2.2"` means `1.2.2` up to but excluding `2.0.0`), which is often tighter than your code needs.

This offer ranking crashes with a `BoundsError` when the same id gets several improving offers:

```julia
mutable struct FixedHeap{T}
    data::Vector{T}
    n::Int
end
FixedHeap{T}(capacity::Integer) where {T} = FixedHeap{T}(Vector{T}(undef, capacity), 0)
Base.isempty(h::FixedHeap) = h.n == 0

function heappush!(h::FixedHeap, x)
    i = (h.n += 1)
    h.data[i] = x
    while i > 1 && h.data[i] < h.data[i >> 1]
        h.data[i], h.data[i >> 1] = h.data[i >> 1], h.data[i]
        i >>= 1
    end
    return h
end

function heappop!(h::FixedHeap)
    top = h.data[1]
    h.data[1] = h.data[h.n]
    h.n -= 1
    i = 1
    while true
        c = 2i
        c > h.n && break
        c < h.n && h.data[c + 1] < h.data[c] && (c += 1)
        h.data[c] < h.data[i] || break
        h.data[c], h.data[i] = h.data[i], h.data[c]
        i = c
    end
    return top
end

function ranked_ids(n::Integer, offers)
    best = Dict{Int,Float64}()
    h = FixedHeap{Tuple{Float64,Int}}(n)
    for (id, cost) in offers
        if cost < get(best, id, Inf)
            best[id] = cost
            heappush!(h, (cost, id))
        end
    end
    out = Int[]
    done = Set{Int}()
    while !isempty(h)
        cost, id = heappop!(h)
        if cost == best[id] && id ∉ done
            push!(out, id)
            push!(done, id)
        end
    end
    return out
end
```

Improving an id's cost pushes a new entry and leaves the old one in the heap (lazy decrease-key). With `n` ids there can be many more than `n` pushes, because each improving offer is a push:

```julia
ranked_ids(3, [(1, 5.0), (2, 4.0)])  # → [2, 1]
ranked_ids(3, [(1, 5.0), (1, 4.0), (1, 3.0), (2, 1.0)])  # → BoundsError: attempt to access 3-element Vector{Tuple{Float64, Int64}} at index [4]
```

The capacity must cover the number of pushes, and that is at most the number of offers:

```julia
mutable struct FixedHeap{T}
    data::Vector{T}
    n::Int
end
FixedHeap{T}(capacity::Integer) where {T} = FixedHeap{T}(Vector{T}(undef, capacity), 0)
Base.isempty(h::FixedHeap) = h.n == 0

function heappush!(h::FixedHeap, x)
    i = (h.n += 1)
    h.data[i] = x
    while i > 1 && h.data[i] < h.data[i >> 1]
        h.data[i], h.data[i >> 1] = h.data[i >> 1], h.data[i]
        i >>= 1
    end
    return h
end

function heappop!(h::FixedHeap)
    top = h.data[1]
    h.data[1] = h.data[h.n]
    h.n -= 1
    i = 1
    while true
        c = 2i
        c > h.n && break
        c < h.n && h.data[c + 1] < h.data[c] && (c += 1)
        h.data[c] < h.data[i] || break
        h.data[c], h.data[i] = h.data[i], h.data[c]
        i = c
    end
    return top
end

function ranked_ids(offers)
    best = Dict{Int,Float64}()
    h = FixedHeap{Tuple{Float64,Int}}(max(1, length(offers)))
    for (id, cost) in offers
        if cost < get(best, id, Inf)
            best[id] = cost
            heappush!(h, (cost, id))
        end
    end
    out = Int[]
    done = Set{Int}()
    while !isempty(h)
        cost, id = heappop!(h)
        if cost == best[id] && id ∉ done
            push!(out, id)
            push!(done, id)
        end
    end
    return out
end

ranked_ids([(1, 5.0), (1, 4.0), (1, 3.0), (2, 1.0)])  # → [2, 1]
```

The signature no longer takes `n`: the number of ids is irrelevant to the bound. If the offers come from a stream with unknown length, use a heap backed by a growing `Vector` instead.
