how do I read a struct C retruns by pointer, one field is `const char *name`, and I dont want to copy the C table

Declare the field as `Cstring` (or `Ptr{UInt8}`), `unsafe_load` the struct from the pointer, and convert the string with `unsafe_string`. Always check for `NULL` first.

```c
typedef struct { const char *name; int32_t value; } entry_t;
const entry_t *entry_at(int i);   // NULL when i is out of range
```

```julia
const libdemo = "./libdemo"

struct Entry
    name::Cstring
    value::Int32
end

function entry(i::Integer)
    p = @ccall libdemo.entry_at(i::Cint)::Ptr{Entry}
    p == C_NULL && throw(BoundsError("entry table", i))
    e = unsafe_load(p)                    # copies the 16-byte struct, not the string
    return (unsafe_string(e.name), e.value)
end

(entry(1), entry(2))
# → (("beta", 2), ("gamma", 3))
```

`unsafe_load` copies the struct; the `Cstring` field is still a pointer into C-owned memory, so convert it with `unsafe_string` before the library can free or overwrite it.
Is it fine to specify the version of my package in `Project.toml` by hand?

Yes. `version` (like `name` and `authors`) is authored data, and Pkg has no command to change it. Dependency data (`[deps]`, `[weakdeps]`, the manifest) is the part to leave to Pkg. `[compat]` is edited either with `Pkg.compat` or by hand.

Before changing the version, read the current `Project.toml` and the latest registered version (for a registered package, the `Versions.toml` file under the registry in your depot lists each registered version), and bump only if the current version has already been released. Commit subjects that say "bump to v0.15" are not evidence of a release.

What does `@simd` actually promise, and when is it wrong to use it?

`@simd` on a `for` loop tells the compiler it may reorder iterations and reassociate floating-point reductions. You are promising that doing so does not change the meaning of your program, other than rounding. It is wrong when iterations depend on each other.

```julia
function seqsum(x)
    s = 0.0
    for v in x
        s += v
    end
    s
end

function simdsum(x)
    s = 0.0
    @simd for v in x
        s += v
    end
    s
end

x = randn(10^5)
seqsum(x) == simdsum(x)       # → false  (different rounding)
isapprox(seqsum(x), simdsum(x))   # → true
abs(sum(x) - simdsum(x)) < 1e-9   # → true (sum may also differ in the last bits)
```

`@simd ivdep` makes a stronger promise: no loop-carried dependencies or aliasing at all. If it is false, the result is wrong without any error:

```julia
function prefix!(a)
    for i in 2:length(a)
        a[i] += a[i-1]       # each element depends on the previous result
    end
    a
end

function prefix_ivdep!(a)
    @simd ivdep for i in 2:length(a)
        a[i] += a[i-1]
    end
    a
end

prefix!(ones(32))[end]         # → 32.0
prefix_ivdep!(ones(32))[end]   # → 5.0
```

On Julia 1.13.2 on my machine `prefix_ivdep!` returned 5.0; the exact wrong value (or, if the loop is not vectorized, the right one) depends on the Julia version and CPU, which is what makes this kind of annotation hard to test.

Use `@simd` on independent elementwise loops and on reductions where rounding changes are acceptable. Use `ivdep` only when you can prove no aliasing between the arrays you read and write. Do not use either on strided scatter loops or loops with a real recurrence.
simple SIR epidemic model wit euler steps, return the trajectory as three vectors

```julia
function sir(beta::Real, gamma::Real, s0::Real, i0::Real; dt::Real = 0.1, tmax::Real = 100)
    (beta >= 0 && gamma >= 0 && dt > 0) || throw(ArgumentError("beta, gamma must be >= 0 and dt > 0"))
    T = float(promote_type(typeof(beta), typeof(gamma), typeof(s0), typeof(i0), typeof(dt)))
    n = round(Int, tmax / dt)
    S, I, R = Vector{T}(undef, n + 1), Vector{T}(undef, n + 1), Vector{T}(undef, n + 1)
    S[1], I[1], R[1] = s0, i0, 1 - s0 - i0
    for k in 1:n
        new_inf = beta * S[k] * I[k] * dt
        new_rec = gamma * I[k] * dt
        S[k+1] = S[k] - new_inf
        I[k+1] = I[k] + new_inf - new_rec
        R[k+1] = R[k] + new_rec
    end
    return S, I, R
end

# Checks
S, I, R = sir(0.5, 0.1, 0.99, 0.01; dt = 0.05, tmax = 200)
@assert all(k -> S[k] + I[k] + R[k] ≈ 1, eachindex(S))
@assert issorted(S; rev = true)
@assert maximum(I) > 0.1
S32, _, _ = sir(0.5f0, 0.1f0, 0.99f0, 0.01f0; dt = 0.1f0, tmax = 10)
@assert eltype(S32) == Float32
```

The three compartments always sum to 1 because every infection removes from S what it adds to I, and every recovery moves from I to R; the test uses this conservation as an invariant. The element type is derived from the inputs, so `Float32` input stays `Float32`. Explicit Euler is fine for illustration; for accuracy use a higher-order solver and a smaller `dt`.

Why does this allocate several temporary arrays, and how do I make it one pass?

```julia
function f(a, b)
    t1 = a .* 2
    t2 = b .^ 2
    return t1 .+ t2
end
```

Each statement materializes an array. A single fused broadcast evaluates the whole expression element by element and allocates only the result, and with `.=` into a preallocated array it allocates nothing:

```julia
f_unfused(a, b) = (t1 = a .* 2; t2 = b .^ 2; t1 .+ t2)
f_fused(a, b)   = a .* 2 .+ b .^ 2                 # one result array
f_fused_at(a, b) = @. a * 2 + b^2                  # same, with @. adding every dot
f_inplace!(c, a, b) = (c .= a .* 2 .+ b .^ 2)      # no result allocation

a, b = rand(10^4), rand(10^4); c = similar(a)
f_unfused(a, b); f_fused(a, b); f_fused_at(a, b); f_inplace!(c, a, b)
@allocated f_unfused(a, b)      # → 240216
@allocated f_fused(a, b)        # → 80072
@allocated f_fused_at(a, b)     # → 80072
@allocated f_inplace!(c, a, b)  # → 0
f_fused(a, b) == f_unfused(a, b)  # → true
```

The unfused version allocates three arrays (three times the 80,000-byte payload of a single result), the fused one allocates one, the in-place one none. Fusion happens at parse time: a chain of dotted operations and `.=` is one loop. A function call like `sum(...)` or an undotted `+` breaks the fusion chain.
how can i evaluate user input like "2 + 3 * (4 - 1)" without eval on arbitrary code

Parse it, then walk the tree yourself with a whitelist of operators. Anything not in the table (function calls, assignments, variables) is rejected, so no arbitrary code runs.

```julia
const OPS = Dict(:+ => +, :- => -, :* => *, :/ => /, :^ => ^)

function calc(ex)
    ex isa Number && return ex
    if Meta.isexpr(ex, :call) && haskey(OPS, ex.args[1])
        return OPS[ex.args[1]](map(calc, ex.args[2:end])...)
    end
    error("not allowed: $ex")
end

println(calc(Meta.parse("2 + 3 * (4 - 1)")))
println(calc(Meta.parse("-2^2")))
r = try
    calc(Meta.parse("exit(1)"))
catch e
    e.msg
end
println(r)
```

Output:

```text
11
-4
not allowed: exit(1)
```

`Meta.parse("(4 - 1)")` yields the inner expression directly (parentheses are not nodes), and unary minus is a `:call` on `:-` with one argument, which the table handles. Note `-2^2` is `-(2^2)` by precedence.
Collatz: find the starting number below a limit with the longest chain, caching chain lengths

```julia
function longest_collatz(limit::Integer)
    limit >= 2 || throw(ArgumentError("limit must be at least 2"))
    cache = zeros(Int, limit)
    cache[1] = 1
    best, best_len = 1, 1
    for start in 2:limit-1
        n, steps = start, 0
        while n >= limit || cache[n] == 0
            n = iseven(n) ? n >> 1 : 3n + 1
            steps += 1
        end
        cache[start] = steps + cache[n]
        if cache[start] > best_len
            best, best_len = start, cache[start]
        end
    end
    return best, best_len
end

# Checks
@assert longest_collatz(10) == (9, 20)
@assert longest_collatz(100) == (97, 119)
@assert longest_collatz(1000) == (871, 179)
@assert longest_collatz(10_000)[1] == 6171
```

Chain lengths for numbers below the limit are memoized in a vector (cheaper than a `Dict`), and a walk stops as soon as it lands on a cached value; values that wander above the limit are simply not cached. This makes the whole computation roughly linear in `limit`. The chain length counts terms including the starting number and the final 1.
got a module of one-shot setup code, is there a module-level way to say dont bother inferring or optimizing it

`Base.Experimental.@compiler_options` sets several compiler flags for the enclosing module at once:

```julia
module Setup
Base.Experimental.@compiler_options compile=min infer=false optimize=0
g(x) = 2x + 1
end
```

- `compile=min` requests the minimum amount of native compilation: the interpreter runs what it can.
- `infer=false` disables type inference for the module, which implies `@nospecialize` on every argument.
- `optimize=0..3` is the same as `@optlevel`.
- `max_methods=1..4` or `default` is the same as `@max_methods` at module scope.

This is the right tool for a module whose functions each run once (build-time configuration, one-off data loading, test setup) and whose compile time is pure waste. It is the wrong tool for anything called in a loop, and it affects only code defined in that module; the functions it calls in other modules keep their own settings.

Caveats:

- `infer=false` means nothing in the module returns a concrete inferred type to its callers. Keep such a module behind a function barrier: hot code should receive concretely typed values from it, not call into it repeatedly.
- The macro is experimental API (present on 1.10 LTS with the same options), so a package that uses it should expect to maintain it.
- Measure first. `@time using MyPkg` and `@time first_call()` in fresh processes, with and without the setting, is the test. If the module's compile time is not a visible part of load latency, leave it alone.
Why does my in-place ODE give a constant solution? I wrote du = -p.k .* u.

`du = ...` creates a new local variable named `du`; the array the solver passed in is untouched, so the derivative the solver sees is whatever was in the buffer (zeros initially) and the solution stays constant. Assign into the existing array:

```julia
using OrdinaryDiffEqTsit5

bad!(du, u, p, t)  = (du = -p.k .* u; nothing)      # rebinds the local name only
good!(du, u, p, t) = (du .= -p.k .* u; nothing)     # writes into the caller's array

for f! in (bad!, good!)
    prob = ODEProblem(f!, [1.0], (0.0, 1.0), (k = 1.0,))
    println(nameof(f!), "  ", solve(prob, Tsit5()).u[end])
end
# bad!   [1.0]
# good!  [0.3678795934275366]
```

Same rule inside any in-place function: `du .= expr`, `du[i] = expr`, or `copyto!(du, expr)`. Another reason to check the result: a constant `sol` for a decaying system is a strong hint of this bug.

Subset sum: is there a subset of integers that adds to target? Positive integers only.

```julia
function subset_sum(v::AbstractVector{<:Integer}, target::Integer)
    all(>(0), v) || throw(ArgumentError("elements must be positive"))
    target >= 0 || return false
    reachable = falses(target + 1)
    reachable[1] = true
    for x in v, s in target:-1:x
        reachable[s+1] |= reachable[s-x+1]
    end
    return reachable[end]
end

# Checks
@assert subset_sum([3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2], 9)
@assert !subset_sum([3, 34, 4, 12, 5, 2], 30)
@assert subset_sum(Int[], 0)
@assert !subset_sum(Int[], 1)
```

A `BitVector` marks which sums are reachable. Iterating sums downward for each element prevents using the same element twice. Time is O(n x target) and memory O(target) bits, so it is pseudo-polynomial: fine for moderate targets, hopeless for huge ones.

Implement `Base.iterate` for the type, plus `length` and `eltype` if they are known. Everything else (`for`, `collect`, `sum`, `map`, `first`) is built on `iterate`.

```julia
struct Countdown
    n::Int
end

Base.iterate(c::Countdown, state = c.n) = state < 1 ? nothing : (state, state - 1)
Base.length(c::Countdown) = c.n
Base.eltype(::Type{Countdown}) = Int

collect(Countdown(3)) # → [3, 2, 1]
sum(Countdown(4))     # → 10
[x^2 for x in Countdown(3)] # → [9, 4, 1]
```

```julia
struct Stream; end
Base.iterate(::Stream, s = 0) = s > 4 ? nothing : (s, s + 1)
Base.eltype(::Type{Stream}) = Int
Base.IteratorSize(::Type{Stream}) = Base.SizeUnknown()
collect(Stream()) # → [0, 1, 2, 3, 4]
```

what does this mean: StringIndexError: invalid index [3], valid nearby indices [2]=>'é', [4]=>'l'

Julia strings are UTF-8 and are indexed by byte position. In `"héllo"`, the character `é` occupies two bytes (positions 2 and 3), so index 3 points into the middle of a character. The error lists the nearest valid starts.

```julia
s = "héllo"
(s[2], nextind(s, 2), length(s), ncodeunits(s), first(s, 3), collect(s)[3])
```

- `length(s)` counts characters (5); `ncodeunits(s)` counts bytes (6).
- `nextind(s, i)` and `prevind(s, i)` step to the next/previous valid character index.
- `first(s, n)` and `last(s, n)` take characters, not bytes.
- `collect(s)` gives a `Vector{Char}` for true character indexing, at the cost of an allocation.

A `BoundsError` on a string (`3-codeunit String at index [10]`) means the byte index is beyond the end. Use `eachindex(s)` to iterate valid indices.

Determinant by cofactor expansion would be exponential. Write a determinant via elimination that returns exact results for integer matrices (use Rational).

```julia
function exact_det(A::AbstractMatrix{<:Integer})
    n = size(A, 1)
    n == size(A, 2) || throw(DimensionMismatch("A must be square, got $(size(A))"))
    M = Rational{BigInt}.(A)
    d = one(Rational{BigInt})
    for k in 1:n
        p = findfirst(i -> !iszero(M[i, k]), k:n)
        p === nothing && return zero(BigInt)
        p += k - 1
        if p != k
            M[[k, p], :] = M[[p, k], :]
            d = -d
        end
        d *= M[k, k]
        for i in k+1:n
            M[i, :] -= (M[i, k] / M[k, k]) * M[k, :]
        end
    end
    return numerator(d)
end

# Checks
@assert exact_det([1 2; 3 4]) == -2
@assert exact_det([2 0 0; 0 3 0; 0 0 4]) == 24
using LinearAlgebra
M = [3 1 4 1; 5 9 2 6; 5 3 5 8; 9 7 9 3]
@assert exact_det(M) == round(Int, det(M))
H = [1 // (i + j - 1) for i in 1:4, j in 1:4]
@assert try exact_det(H); false catch e; e isa MethodError end
```

Row reduction over `Rational{BigInt}` is exact: no rounding error and no overflow, and the determinant of an integer matrix is an integer, so the result is the numerator. Row swaps flip the sign and the determinant is the product of the pivots. Floating-point `det` can return `-2.0000000000000004`, which is why exact arithmetic matters for integer problems. The last check shows rational matrices are intentionally rejected by the signature.

slow on big files, why

```julia
function count_hits(lines, word)
    n = 0
    for l in lines
        n += occursin(Regex("\\b" * word * "\\b"), l)
    end
    n
end
```

`Regex(...)` compiles the pattern each time it is called. Building it inside the loop recompiles the identical pattern for every line. Build it once:

```julia

    rx = Regex("\\b" * word * "\\b")
```

```julia

fast(lines, w) = (rx = Regex("\\b" * w * "\\b"); count(l -> occursin(rx, l), lines))
lines = fill("xx aab xx", 2000)
slow(lines, "aab"); fast(lines, "aab")
@elapsed(slow(lines, "aab")) > 5 * @elapsed(fast(lines, "aab"))  # → true
```

My data fits in Float32. How much memory does that save, and is it safe?

Half for floats (4 vs 8 bytes per element), and a quarter or an eighth for small integers:

```julia
n = 10^6
(Base.summarysize(zeros(Float64, n)),
 Base.summarysize(zeros(Float32, n)),
 Base.summarysize(zeros(Int8, n)))
```

That is about 8 MB, 4 MB and 1 MB. Safety depends on the numerics: `Float32` has about 7 significant digits, so long accumulations, ill-conditioned solves and differences of nearly equal numbers can lose accuracy. A common pattern is to store in `Float32` and accumulate in `Float64`: `sum(Float64, x32)` converts element by element without a temporary `Float64` array. Integer types overflow silently, so check the range first (`typemax(Int8)` is 127).

no temporaries please

```julia
dist(x, y) = sqrt(sum(abs2, x .- y))
```

`x .- y` allocates a full-size temporary. Fold the difference into the reduction with an index loop or a generator over `eachindex(x, y)`; the second argument also checks that the axes agree:

```julia
using LinearAlgebra

dist_tmp(x, y) = sqrt(sum(abs2, x .- y))
dist(x, y) = sqrt(sum(i -> abs2(x[i] - y[i]), eachindex(x, y)))

x, y = randn(10^4), randn(10^4)
dist_tmp(x, y); dist(x, y); norm(x - y)
@allocated dist_tmp(x, y)     # → 80072
@allocated dist(x, y)         # → 0
@allocated norm(x - y)        # → 80088
dist(x, y) ≈ dist_tmp(x, y) ≈ norm(x - y)   # → true
```

The temporary-free version is typically several times faster. Both `x - y` and `x .- y` allocate; only the fused-into-the-reduction form does not. If you need a numerically careful 2-norm (scaling against overflow), `norm` is the right function and the temporary is a fair price.

```julia
struct Temperature
    kelvin::Float64
    function Temperature(kelvin::Real)
        kelvin >= 0 || throw(ArgumentError("temperature below absolute zero: $kelvin K"))
        new(kelvin)
    end
end

celsius(c::Real) = Temperature(c + 273.15)
fahrenheit(f::Real) = Temperature((f - 32) * 5 / 9 + 273.15)
to_celsius(t::Temperature) = t.kelvin - 273.15
to_fahrenheit(t::Temperature) = (t.kelvin - 273.15) * 9 / 5 + 32

Base.isless(a::Temperature, b::Temperature) = a.kelvin < b.kelvin
Base.show(io::IO, t::Temperature) = print(io, round(to_celsius(t); digits = 2), " °C")

# Checks

@assert isapprox(to_celsius(fahrenheit(32)), 0; atol = 1e-12)
@assert maximum([celsius(5), celsius(30), celsius(-10)]) == celsius(30)
@assert try celsius(-300); false catch e; e isa ArgumentError end
```

A colleague uses `a[-1]` and `a[1:3]` expecting Python semantics. What are the differences?

Julia does not support negative indices; use `end`. Slices are inclusive on both ends and start at 1.

```julia
a = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]

a[end]          # → 50
a[end-1]        # → 40
a[1:3]          # → [10, 20, 30]
a[2:end]        # → [20, 30, 40, 50]
a[1:2:end]      # → [10, 30, 50]
a[-1]           # → BoundsError: attempt to access 5-element Vector{Int64} at index [-1]
```

- Python `a[0:3]` (three elements) is `a[1:3]` in Julia.
- Python `a[::2]` is `a[1:2:end]`.
- Python `a[::-1]` is `reverse(a)` or `a[end:-1:1]`.
- `a[a .> 20]` selects by a Boolean mask, as in NumPy.
- In generic code use `a[begin]` and `a[end]`, so `OffsetArray`s work as well.

```julia
reverse(a) # → [50, 40, 30, 20, 10]
a[a .> 20] # → [30, 40, 50]
```

Write `quadratic_roots(a, b, c)` for real roots of ax^2+bx+c that stays accurate when b is huge relative to a and c (the small root must not collapse to zero). Float32 coefficients should give Float32 roots. Reject a == 0 and complex roots with clear exceptions.

```julia
function quadratic_roots(a::Real, b::Real, c::Real)
    T = float(promote_type(typeof(a), typeof(b), typeof(c)))
    a, b, c = T(a), T(b), T(c)
    iszero(a) && throw(ArgumentError("a must be nonzero for a quadratic, got a = $a"))
    disc = b * b - 4 * a * c
    disc < 0 && throw(DomainError(disc, "discriminant is negative: roots are complex"))
    # q has the same sign as b, so b and the square root add instead of cancelling.
    q = -(b + copysign(sqrt(disc), b)) / 2
    r1 = q / a
    r2 = iszero(q) ? r1 : c / q
    return minmax(r1, r2)
end

# Checks
lo, hi = quadratic_roots(1.0, -3.0, 2.0)

lo32, hi32 = quadratic_roots(1.0f0, 1.0f4, 1.0f0)
@assert isapprox(hi32, -1.0f-4; rtol = 1.0f-5)

@assert quadratic_roots(1, 0, 0) == (0.0, 0.0)          # Int input gives Float64

err = try quadratic_roots(0.0, 1.0, 1.0); nothing catch e; e end
@assert err isa ArgumentError && occursin("nonzero", err.msg)
err = try quadratic_roots(1.0, 0.0, 1.0); nothing catch e; e end
@assert err isa DomainError && occursin("complex", err.msg)
```

Of the two textbook forms `(-b ± sqrt(disc)) / 2a`, one subtracts two nearly equal numbers when `b^2 >> 4ac`. Computing the larger-magnitude root from `q` and the other from the product of roots `c / q` avoids that subtraction. `T = float(promote_type(...))` makes the working type follow the inputs, so `Float32` stays `Float32`. The two failure cases are different mistakes by the caller, so they get different exception types.

first solve in session super slow, later ones fast why

Julia compiles the solver for each concrete combination of problem type, algorithm, and state type the first time it is called. That compile cost is paid once per session (and per new type combination), not per solve. Practical consequences:

- Benchmark only after a warm-up call, and use `BenchmarkTools`: `@btime solve($prob, Tsit5())`. Never time the first call.
- Use a persistent session (`julia_create_session`, then `julia_eval_code` repeatedly) so compiled code survives between your edits.
- Changing something that alters the problem's type (a `Float32` `u0`, a different `p` structure, an `SVector` instead of a `Vector`) triggers a new compile, which is why parameter sweeps should keep `p` the same type through `remake`.
- Sublibraries (`OrdinaryDiffEqTsit5`) reduce load time, but do not remove the first-solve compile.

A quick check that it is compile time: call `solve(prob, Tsit5())` twice and time both with `@time`.

```julia
function rot(s::AbstractString, k::Integer)
    io = IOBuffer()
    for c in s
        if 'a' <= c <= 'z'
            print(io, Char(mod(c - 'a' + k, 26) + 'a'))
        elseif 'A' <= c <= 'Z'
            print(io, Char(mod(c - 'A' + k, 26) + 'A'))
        else
            print(io, c)
        end
    end
    return String(take!(io))
end

# Checks
@assert rot("Hello, World!", 13) == "Uryyb, Jbeyq!"
@assert rot("Hello, Ñandú! 日本 €", 13) == "Uryyb, Ñnaqú! 日本 €"
@assert rot("abc", -3) == "xyz"
s = "Zebra ñ, café, 日本語 ☃"
@assert length(rot(s, 7)) == length(s)
```

Output goes through `print(io, c)`, which writes the character's UTF-8 encoding; do not use `write(io, c)` on bytes you converted to `Char`, because a `Char` above `0x7f` is written as two or more bytes.

How do I send a length-prefixed binary message over a socket?

Write a fixed-size header (here an `Int32` byte count), then the payload. The receiver reads exactly the header size, then exactly that many bytes. Mind byte order if the peers differ; `hton`/`ntoh` convert to and from network order.

```julia
using Sockets

server = listen(ip"127.0.0.1", 0)
port = getsockname(server)[2]
srv = @async begin
    s = accept(server)
    n = ntoh(read(s, Int32))
    data = read(s, n)                # exactly n bytes
    write(s, hton(Int32(sum(data))))
    close(s)
end

c = connect(port)
payload = UInt8[1, 2, 3, 4]
write(c, hton(Int32(length(payload))))
write(c, payload)
total = ntoh(read(c, Int32))
close(c); wait(srv); close(server)
total
```

This returns `10`. `read(s, n)` returns a `Vector{UInt8}` of length `n` and returns fewer bytes than requested if the peer closes early, so check `length` before trusting it.

I'll keep per-thread buffers indexed by `threadid()`. Standard practice, right?

```julia
buffers = [zeros(100) for _ in 1:nthreads()]
@threads for i in 1:1000
    b = buffers[threadid()]
    # ... use b ...
end
```

Not safe in current Julia. Tasks can migrate between threads at yield points, so `threadid()` can change inside the loop body, and there can be more thread ids than `nthreads()` (an interactive thread pool adds one). In my session with 16 default threads, a loop indexing a `nthreads()`-length vector by `threadid()` failed with a `BoundsError` at index 17.

Use one buffer per task or per chunk instead:

```julia
using Base.Threads

function work!(results, chunks)
    @sync for (c, idx) in enumerate(chunks)
        Threads.@spawn begin
            buf = zeros(100)                 # task-local, allocated once per chunk
            acc = 0.0
            for i in idx
                buf .= i                     # ... use buf ...
                acc += sum(buf)
            end
            results[c] = acc
        end
    end
    results
end

chunks = collect(Iterators.partition(1:1000, 100))
results = zeros(length(chunks))
work!(results, chunks)
sum(results) == sum(100.0 * i for i in 1:1000)   # → true
```

Each task writes only its own slot `results[c]`, so there is no race. For reusable buffers across calls, keep a pool (a `Channel` of buffers) and take/put them per task.

```julia
`log(sum(exp, x))` computed after subtracting the maximum, so large entries do
not overflow. Throws `ArgumentError` for an empty collection.
"""
function logsumexp(x::AbstractArray{<:Real})
    isempty(x) && throw(ArgumentError("logsumexp of an empty collection"))
    m = maximum(x)
    isinf(m) && return float(m)
    return m + log(sum(v -> exp(v - m), x))
end

"Normalized `exp.(x)`, computed stably."
function softmax(x::AbstractArray{<:Real})
    e = exp.(x .- maximum(x))
    return e ./ sum(e)
end

end # module
```

`mean` of my data returns `missing` or `NaN` and also how do I deal with empty inputs

`mean` propagates `missing` and `NaN` exactly like arithmetic. Wrap in `skipmissing` to drop missing values; drop NaNs with `filter(!isnan, x)`. Empty inputs differ: `mean` of an empty `Float64` array is `NaN`, while `median` throws.

```julia
using Statistics

x = [1.0, 2.0, missing, 4.0]
e = Float64[]

(mean(x), mean(skipmissing(x)), median(skipmissing(x)),
 mean([1, NaN, 3]), mean(filter(!isnan, [1, NaN, 3])),
 isnan(mean(e)), try median(e) catch err; sprint(showerror, err) end)
```

The result is `(missing, 2.3333333333333335, 2.0, NaN, 2.0, true, "ArgumentError: median of an empty array is undefined, Float64[]")`. If every value may be missing, test `isempty(collect(skipmissing(x)))` before taking statistics.
Recursive-descent parser and evaluator for arithmetic with + - * / parentheses and unary minus. Input is a string. No eval.

```julia
function calc(src::AbstractString)
    s = filter(!isspace, src)
    pos = 1
    peek() = pos <= lastindex(s) ? s[pos] : '\0'
    function number()
        start = pos
        while peek() in "0123456789."
            pos += 1
        end
        start == pos && throw(ArgumentError("expected a number at position $pos in \"$src\""))
        return parse(Float64, s[start:pos-1])
    end
    function factor()
        if peek() == '-'
            pos += 1
            return -factor()
        elseif peek() == '('
            pos += 1
            v = expr()
            peek() == ')' || throw(ArgumentError("missing ')' in \"$src\""))
            pos += 1
            return v
        end
        return number()
    end
    function term()
        v = factor()
        while peek() in "*/"
            op = peek(); pos += 1
            r = factor()
            v = op == '*' ? v * r : v / r
        end
        return v
    end
    function expr()
        v = term()
        while peek() in "+-"
            op = peek(); pos += 1
            r = term()
            v = op == '+' ? v + r : v - r
        end
        return v
    end
    result = expr()
    pos > lastindex(s) || throw(ArgumentError("unexpected '$(peek())' at position $pos in \"$src\""))
    return result
end

# Checks
@assert calc("1 + 2 * 3") == 7
@assert calc("10 - 4 - 3") == 3                 # left-associative
@assert try calc("(1 + 2"); false catch e; e isa ArgumentError end
@assert try calc("1 (2)"); false catch e; e isa ArgumentError end
```

Each grammar rule becomes one function (`expr` -> `term` -> `factor`), which encodes precedence: `*` and `/` bind tighter because `term` sits below `expr`. Loops in `expr` and `term` give left associativity. Parsing instead of calling `eval(Meta.parse(...))` keeps untrusted input from executing arbitrary code. Errors report the position within the input with whitespace removed.
Write a macro `@timeit expr` that evaluates `expr` and returns a named tuple with its value and elapsed seconds, without clobbering user variables.

Use temporaries from the macro's own quote, which are hygienic and cannot collide with the user's names, and return the result as the last expression.

```julia
macro timeit(ex)
    return quote
        t0 = time_ns()
        result = $(esc(ex))
        t1 = time_ns()
        (; value = result, seconds = (t1 - t0) / 1e9)
    end
end

t0 = "user's variable"
result = "user's result"
r = @timeit sum(1:1000)
println(r.value, " ", r.seconds >= 0)
println(t0, "; ", result)
```

Output:

```text
500500 true
user's variable; user's result
```

The user's `t0` and `result` are untouched because the macro's own `t0` and `result` are renamed. For benchmarking use BenchmarkTools or Chairmarks: a single `time_ns` measurement includes compilation on the first call.

Use summaries instead of printing the frame.

Bit manipulation helpers: popcount, is a power of two, lowest set bit, and Gray code conversion

```julia
popcount(x::Integer) = count_ones(x)
is_pow2(x::Integer) = x > 0 && (x & (x - 1)) == 0
lowest_set_bit(x::Integer) = x & -x
to_gray(x::Unsigned) = x ⊻ (x >> 1)

function from_gray(g::Unsigned)
    x = g
    while (g >>= 1) != 0
        x ⊻= g
    end
    return x
end

# Checks
@assert popcount(0b10110) == 3 && popcount(0) == 0
@assert lowest_set_bit(0b101000) == 0b1000
@assert [to_gray(UInt8(i)) for i in 0:7] == UInt8[0, 1, 3, 2, 6, 7, 5, 4]
@assert all(count_ones(to_gray(UInt8(i)) ⊻ to_gray(UInt8(i + 1))) == 1 for i in 0:254)
```

`x & (x - 1)` clears the lowest set bit, so a power of two (one set bit) becomes zero; `x & -x` isolates that bit using two's complement. Consecutive Gray codes differ in exactly one bit, which the last assertion checks over the whole `UInt8` range. `count_ones` compiles to the hardware popcount instruction where available.
How do I get just the installed version of an external tool, and fail fast if it's too old?

Resolve the tool, run its version flag, parse the version number with a regex, and compare with `VersionNumber`.

```julia
function tool_version(name::AbstractString, flag = "--version")
    exe = Sys.which(name)
    exe === nothing && error("`$name` not found on PATH")
    out = readchomp(pipeline(`$exe $flag`; stderr = devnull))      # some tools print to stderr; adapt per tool
    m = match(r"(\d+)\.(\d+)(?:\.(\d+))?", out)
    m === nothing && error("could not parse a version from the output of `$name $flag`: ", repr(out))
    return VersionNumber(parse(Int, m[1]), parse(Int, m[2]), m[3] === nothing ? 0 : parse(Int, m[3]))
end

function require_version(name, minimum::VersionNumber)
    v = tool_version(name)
    v >= minimum || error("`$name` $v is older than the required $minimum")
    return v
end

v = tool_version("sort")
v isa VersionNumber        # → true
```

Cache the result instead of probing on every call. Match the regex to the tool's actual output format, because tools differ (and some print their version to stderr). For a library, the equivalent is a version function in its API (`zlibVersion`, `ZSTD_versionNumber`), which is more reliable than parsing text.
Show a basic EnsembleProblem for a parameter sweep.

In recent SciMLBase (the version I checked was 3.53) `prob_func` takes `(prob, ctx)`, where `ctx.sim_id` is the trajectory index. Older code used `(prob, i, repeat)`; that three-argument form throws a `MethodError` on this version.

```julia
using OrdinaryDiffEqTsit5

decay!(du, u, p, t) = (du[1] = -p.k * u[1]; nothing)
prob = ODEProblem(decay!, [1.0], (0.0, 5.0), (k = 1.0,))
ks = [0.5, 1.0, 2.0]

ens = EnsembleProblem(prob; prob_func = (prob, ctx) -> remake(prob, p = (k = ks[ctx.sim_id],)))
sim = solve(ens, Tsit5(), EnsembleThreads(); trajectories = length(ks))

[s.u[end][1] for s in sim.u]
# → [0.0820857484865343, 0.006738503575123539, 4.543479057358619e-5]
sim.converged   # → true
```

`EnsembleSerial()` runs sequentially; `EnsembleThreads()` uses Julia threads (start Julia with `-t` for more than one). Index results through `sim.u`: each element is a full solution. If your `f!` touches shared global state it is not safe to run threaded.
I'm replacing a hand-tuned kernel with a generated one. It's faster than the library baseline, so it passes the benchmark gate.

The gate that matters for a replacement is the kernel you are replacing, not the library floor. A generated kernel can clear the library baseline and still be a large regression against the hand-tuned code it replaces.

Measure three things on warmed-up inputs:

- generated vs the current hand-tuned kernel (par or better is the bar),
- generated vs a reference implementation for correctness,
- both against the library floor, which should hold automatically if the first holds.

If the generated one is slower than the current kernel, the replacement fails regardless of the library comparison. If it is faster, the hand-tuned one was sub-optimal, which is also worth recording.
I preallocate my priority queue with one slot per node and use lazy deletion (push a fresh entry whenever a node's priority improves, skip stale entries when popped). Is one slot per node enough?

No. With lazy deletion the queue holds one entry per push, and a node can be pushed once for every time its priority improves. The safe bound is the total number of pushes:

- For a graph search where every node is expanded at most once and each expansion pushes at most one entry per outgoing edge, the bound is the number of directed edges (plus 1 for the start entry).
- For a stream of updates, it is the number of updates.

A `BoundsError` on the push means the bound was too small. Three ways out:

1. Size the buffer from the bound above and state the bound in a comment.
2. Use a growable heap (`push!` onto a `Vector` and sift up). Amortized growth is cheap, and a failed bound cannot occur.
3. Implement a real decrease-key with a position index (`pos[node]`), which keeps one entry per node and makes `n` slots sufficient, at the cost of maintaining the index on every swap.

Keep the precondition testable: a test with a dense graph (every pair connected) and many equal improvements exercises exactly the case where `n` slots run out.
One sentence only: why is the first call of a Julia function slower than the later calls?
The first call with a given combination of argument types has to compile a specialized method, and later calls with the same types reuse that compiled code.
Why does a `Threads.@spawn` closure sometimes see a value I changed after spawning it?

A spawned closure captures variables, not values. A loop variable is fresh per iteration, but a variable declared outside and reassigned is shared, so the task may see a later value. Interpolate with `$` to copy the value at spawn time.

```julia
function demo()
    x = 0
    tasks = Task[]
    for i in 1:3
        x = i
        push!(tasks, Threads.@spawn $x * 10)   # $x is evaluated now
    end
    println(fetch.(tasks))

    y = 0
    t = Threads.@spawn (sleep(0.05); y)        # reads y when it runs
    y = 5
    println(fetch(t))
end
demo()
```

`$x` in `@spawn` captures the current value at task creation. Without it, the second task reads `y` after `y = 5`, so the result is 5, not 0.

Param struct treated as collection in broadcast, length error

```julia
struct Cfg
    k::Int
end
add(x, c) = x + c.k
add.(1:3, Cfg(5))
```

Broadcasting treats an argument as a container unless `Base.broadcastable` says otherwise. Numbers, strings, symbols, and functions are scalars already; an unknown struct is handed to `axes`/`length`, which it does not have. Opt in to scalar behavior by wrapping the value in a `Ref`:

```julia
struct Cfg
    k::Int
end
add(x, c) = x + c.k

e = try add.(1:3, Cfg(5)) catch err; first(sprint(showerror, err), 55) end
Base.broadcastable(c::Cfg) = Ref(c)
(e, add.(1:3, Cfg(5)))
```

The result is `("MethodError: no method matching length(::Main.Cfg)...", [6, 7, 8])` (the exact module prefix depends on where you define it). Without the method you can also write `add.(1:3, Ref(Cfg(5)))` at each call site, but defining `broadcastable` once is the supported way to make a type behave as a scalar.
My threaded code that calls `mul!` in every thread became slower after I added threads. Why?

Large dense matrix products in Julia call BLAS, which is itself multithreaded. If every Julia thread calls BLAS, the total number of runnable threads is Julia threads × BLAS threads and they fight for the cores. When Julia-level parallelism is the outer loop, set BLAS to one thread.

```julia
using LinearAlgebra
println(BLAS.get_num_threads() >= 1)
old = BLAS.get_num_threads()
BLAS.set_num_threads(1)
println(BLAS.get_num_threads())

As = [rand(100, 100) for _ in 1:8]
Cs = [similar(A) for A in As]
Threads.@threads for i in eachindex(As, Cs)
    mul!(Cs[i], As[i], As[i])      # single-threaded BLAS call per Julia thread
end
println(all(Cs[i] ≈ As[i] * As[i] for i in eachindex(As)))
BLAS.set_num_threads(old)
```

Conversely, if you run one large matrix product at a time, leave BLAS threads at the default and keep the Julia-level work serial. Whether the combination is faster is machine-dependent, so benchmark both settings with `BenchmarkTools` rather than assuming.
Hi, in my code I do x = inv(A) * b in many places and a colleague told me that I should rather write A \ b. Does this really matter or is it only style?

Yes. Use `A \ b`. It factorizes `A` once and does two triangular solves; `inv(A) * b` computes the full inverse (about three times the flops of an LU factorization), allocates an n-by-n matrix, and is typically less accurate.

```julia
using LinearAlgebra, BenchmarkTools
BLAS.set_num_threads(1)
A = [i == j ? 4.0 : 1 / (1 + abs(i - j)) for i in 1:600, j in 1:600]
b = A * ones(600)
t_inv   = @belapsed inv($A) * $b seconds=0.3
t_ldiv  = @belapsed $A \ $b seconds=0.3
a_inv   = @allocated inv(A) * b
a_ldiv  = @allocated A \ b
(inv_slower = t_inv > t_ldiv, inv_allocates_more = a_inv > a_ldiv)
```

```text
(inv_slower = true, inv_allocates_more = true)
```

The first field says `inv` is slower on this run (the size of the gap varies by machine and with `n`); the second says it allocates more. Only form the inverse when you need its entries, for example a covariance diagonal. For a row vector, write `b' / A` instead of `b' * inv(A)`.
I have a script with some functions and a few println calls at the bottom. How do I turn it into a package?

Five mechanical steps.

1. Create the skeleton from the directory that should contain it: `Pkg.generate("Zscores")`. Do not write `Project.toml` yourself.
2. Move the function definitions into the module in `src/Zscores.jl` and `export` only what callers need.
3. Add each library the script `using`ed to the package environment: `Pkg.activate("Zscores")`, then `Pkg.add("Statistics")` (and `Pkg.compat` for registered packages, plus `Pkg.compat("julia", "1.10")`).
4. Turn the `println` checks at the bottom into `@testitem` blocks in `test/`, with real assertions, plus the two-line `test/runtests.jl` (`using TestItemRunner; @run_package_tests`).
5. Keep a thin driver script, if you still want one, that does `using Zscores` and calls the API with your real data.

Result for a script that only had `zscore`:

```julia
# src/Zscores.jl
module Zscores

using Statistics: mean, std

export zscore

"""
    zscore(x)

Standardize `x` to zero mean and unit sample standard deviation.
"""
zscore(x::AbstractArray{<:Real}) = (x .- mean(x)) ./ std(x)

end # module

Zscores.zscore([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
# → [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0]
```

```julia

@testitem "standardizes" begin
    z = zscore([1.0, 2.0, 3.0])
    @test z == [-1.0, 0.0, 1.0]
end
```

When should I use `dump` and when `Meta.show_sexpr`? Show both on `a + b * 2`.

`dump` prints the full typed tree, one field per line, which is the right tool when you need to see exactly which node types and heads you have (`Symbol` vs `QuoteNode` vs literal). `Meta.show_sexpr` prints a compact Lisp-style form, handy for seeing nesting at a glance.

```julia
ex = :(a + b * 2)
dump(ex)
Meta.show_sexpr(ex)
println()
```

Output:

```text
Expr
  head: Symbol call
  args: Array{Any}((3,))
    1: Symbol +
    2: Symbol a
    3: Expr
      head: Symbol call
      args: Array{Any}((3,))
        1: Symbol *
        2: Symbol b
        3: Int64 2
(:call, :+, :a, (:call, :*, :b, 2))
```

What is `strides` and `unsafe_convert` for? When my custom array need to have them

They describe memory layout for code that passes the array to C or BLAS. `strides(A)` gives the element step along each dimension, and `Base.unsafe_convert(Ptr{T}, A)` gives the address of the first element. A custom array type only needs them if it must be accepted where a `StridedArray` is expected (for `ccall` or BLAS routines).

```julia
A = reshape(collect(1:12), 3, 4)
V = view(A, 1:2:3, 2:4)
(strides(A), strides(V), stride(A, 2), strides(A'), pointer(A, 2) - pointer(A),
 try strides(view(A, [1, 3], :)) catch e; typeof(e) end)
```

The result is `((1, 3), (2, 3), 3, (3, 1), 0x0000000000000008, ArgumentError)`: a view with an index vector is not strided, so `strides` throws. A wrapper over contiguous memory implements the two methods plus `elsize`:

```julia
using LinearAlgebra

struct Buf <: DenseVector{Float64}
    p::Vector{Float64}
end
Base.size(b::Buf) = size(b.p)
Base.getindex(b::Buf, i::Int) = b.p[i]
Base.strides(::Buf) = (1,)
Base.unsafe_convert(::Type{Ptr{Float64}}, b::Buf) = Base.unsafe_convert(Ptr{Float64}, b.p)
Base.elsize(::Type{Buf}) = sizeof(Float64)

b = Buf([3.0, 4.0])
(BLAS.nrm2(2, b, 1), BLAS.dot(2, b, 1, b, 1))
```

This returns `(5.0, 25.0)`. Keep the wrapped vector reachable (`GC.@preserve`) in any code that stores the raw pointer.
How do I design an abstract type with a type parameter and write functions against it?

Put the parameter on the abstract type so every subtype exposes it, then extract it with `where` in signatures.

```julia
abstract type AbstractSolver{T<:AbstractFloat} end

struct Newton{T} <: AbstractSolver{T}
    tol::T
    maxiter::Int
end
Newton(; tol = 1e-8, maxiter = 50) = Newton(tol, maxiter)

struct Bisection{T} <: AbstractSolver{T}
    tol::T
end

precision(::AbstractSolver{T}) where {T} = T
tolerance(s::AbstractSolver) = s.tol

precision(Newton())              # → Float64
precision(Bisection(1f-4))       # → Float32
tolerance(Newton(tol = 1e-6))    # → 1.0e-6
```

Subtype parameters are inferred from the constructor arguments (`Newton(1f-4, 10)` is `Newton{Float32}`). The abstract type carries only what all subtypes share, here the floating-point type; shared behavior lives in functions on `AbstractSolver`, and each concrete type adds its own methods. Keep abstract types free of fields. Default `Newton(; tol, maxiter)` above is an outer constructor that computes the parameter from the keyword value.
Write a bisection root finder `bisect(f, lo, hi)`. It should terminate for Float32 as well as Float64 without a hand-picked tolerance, and reject intervals where f does not change sign.

```julia
function bisect(f, lo::Real, hi::Real)
    lo < hi || throw(ArgumentError("need lo < hi, got lo = $lo, hi = $hi"))
    T = float(promote_type(typeof(lo), typeof(hi)))
    a, b = T(lo), T(hi)
    fa, fb = f(a), f(b)
    iszero(fa) && return a
    iszero(fb) && return b
    sign(fa) == sign(fb) &&
        throw(ArgumentError("f must change sign on [$lo, $hi]: f(lo) = $fa, f(hi) = $fb"))
    while true
        m = a + (b - a) / 2
        # Stop when the midpoint is no longer strictly inside: a and b are adjacent floats.
        (m <= a || m >= b) && return m
        fm = f(m)
        iszero(fm) && return m
        if sign(fm) == sign(fa)
            a, fa = m, fm
        else
            b, fb = m, fm
        end
    end
end

# Checks
r = bisect(x -> x^2 - 2, 0.0f0, 2.0f0)
@assert r isa Float32 && abs(r - sqrt(2.0f0)) <= eps(Float32)
r = bisect(x -> x^2 - 2, 0, 2)
@assert r isa Float64 && abs(r - sqrt(2.0)) <= eps(Float64)
@assert bisect(x -> x - 1, 1, 3) == 1.0                    # root at an endpoint

for (lo, hi, pat) in ((1.0, 2.0, "change sign"), (2.0, 1.0, "lo < hi"))
    err = try bisect(x -> x^2 + 1, lo, hi); nothing catch e; e end
    @assert err isa ArgumentError && occursin(pat, err.msg)
end
```

Each halving either shrinks the bracket or finds that the midpoint equals an endpoint, which only happens once the bracket is two adjacent floats of whatever type `T` is, so the loop always terminates and the answer is as accurate as `T` allows. No tolerance argument is needed. `T = float(promote_type(...))` makes `Int` and `Rational` endpoints work and keeps `Float32` endpoints in `Float32`.
My script prints `Sys.maxrss()` after I freed everything and it is still large. Is there a leak?

Not necessarily. `Sys.maxrss()` is the high-water mark, so it cannot decrease. Read the current RSS instead:

```julia
function rss_mb()
    for l in eachline("/proc/self/status")        # Linux
        startswith(l, "VmRSS:") && return parse(Int, split(l)[2]) / 1024
    end
end
rss_mb() > 0
```

`VmHWM` in the same file is the peak (what `Sys.maxrss()` reports), `VmRSS` is now. Compare `VmRSS` before and after `x = nothing; GC.gc()`, and compare `Base.gc_live_bytes()` to separate "Julia still holds it" from "Julia freed it but the allocator kept the pages".
Does `logdet` work on a sparse Cholesky factorization?

Yes: `logdet(F)` for a `cholesky(A)` factorization is cheap (computed from the diagonal of the factor). It is the right quantity for Gaussian log-likelihoods; `det(A)` of a big matrix over- or underflows.

```julia
using SparseArrays, LinearAlgebra
A = sparse([4.0 1 0 0; 1 4 1 0; 0 1 4 1; 0 0 1 4])
F = cholesky(A)
(logdet(F) ≈ logdet(Matrix(A)), isfinite(logdet(F)))
```

```text
(true, true)
```

The determinant of a dense Cholesky works the same way: `logdet(cholesky(Symmetric(A)))`. For an LU factorization use `logabsdet`.

Declare `Base.SizeUnknown()`; `collect` then grows the output as it goes. Do not define a `length` that lies, since `collect` and `zip` may trust it.

```julia
struct Evens

end
Base.iterate(e::Evens, s=2) = s > e.lim ? nothing : (s, s + 2)
Base.IteratorSize(::Type{Evens}) = Base.SizeUnknown()
Base.eltype(::Type{Evens}) = Int

v = collect(Evens(10))
(v, typeof(v), sum(Evens(10)), count(iseven, Evens(10)), maximum(Evens(10)))
```

The result is `([2, 4, 6, 8, 10], Vector{Int64}, 30, 5, 10)`. Reductions never need the length. If the shape is multidimensional and known, use `Base.HasShape{N}()` and define `size`.

why does total return Any, i only use a global array

```julia
data = rand(1000)

function total()
    s = 0.0
    for i in eachindex(data)
        s += data[i]
    end
    s
end
```

`data` is a non-constant global. Any function that reads it must assume its type can change at any moment, so every access is `Any`. Three fixes, best first:

```julia
# 1. pass it as an argument (best: also makes the function reusable)
function total(data)
    s = zero(eltype(data))
    for i in eachindex(data)
        s += data[i]
    end
    s
end

# 2. make the global a constant
const DATA = rand(1000)
function total_const()
    s = 0.0
    for i in eachindex(DATA)
        s += DATA[i]
    end
    s
end

# 3. give the global a type (works, but still a global)
typed::Vector{Float64} = rand(1000)
function total_typed()
    s = 0.0
    for i in eachindex(typed)
        s += typed[i]
    end
    s
end

Base.return_types(total, (Vector{Float64},))    # → Any[Float64]
Base.return_types(total_const, ())              # → Any[Float64]
Base.return_types(total_typed, ())              # → Any[Float64]
```

For the untyped version, `Base.return_types` gives `Any[Any]` and it allocates on every call. It is typically orders of magnitude slower than the `const` version, while typed globals are close to it; measure to confirm. Passing arguments is the idiom that never needs a decision.
How should I write the constructors for a parametric struct so `MyStruct(1, 2.0)`, `MyStruct{Float64}(1, 2)` and `MyStruct{Float64,Float64}(1, 2)` all work and coerce the same way?

Write the inner constructor with unconstrained arguments and let the field types coerce via `new`. Outer constructors only compute type parameters and call inward, forming a cascade.

```julia
struct Pair2{A,B}
    first::A
    second::B
    Pair2{A,B}(first, second) where {A,B} = new{A,B}(first, second)
end

Pair2{A}(first, second) where {A} = Pair2{A,typeof(second)}(first, second)
Pair2(first, second) = Pair2{typeof(first)}(first, second)

Pair2(1, 2.0)               # → Pair2{Int64, Float64}(1, 2.0)
Pair2{Float64}(1, 2)        # → Pair2{Float64, Int64}(1.0, 2)
Pair2{Float64,Float64}(1, 2) # → Pair2{Float64, Float64}(1.0, 2.0)
```

In the inner constructor, `new{A,B}(first, second)` converts `first` to `A` and `second` to `B` through the field declarations, so every call form coerces identically. Do not annotate the inner constructor's value arguments as `(first::A, second::B)`; that rejects `Pair2{Float64,Float64}(1, 2)`:

```julia
struct Strict{A,B}
    first::A
    second::B
    Strict{A,B}(first::A, second::B) where {A,B} = new{A,B}(first, second)
end
```

```text
MethodError: no method matching Strict{Float64, Float64}(::Int64, ::Int64)
The type `Strict{Float64, Float64}` exists, but no method is defined for this combination of argument types when trying to construct it.

Closest candidates are:
  Strict{A, B}(::A, ::B) where {A, B}

```

After a crash in the middle of an append, the next run reads the log and fails (or returns wrong values), even though we reopen it in append mode. Records are `id::Int64, length::UInt32, payload`:

```julia
const TOMBSTONE = typemax(UInt32)

function log_put!(io::IO, id::Int64, value::AbstractString)
    n = ncodeunits(value)
    n < TOMBSTONE || throw(ArgumentError("value too large: $n bytes"))
    write(io, id, UInt32(n), value)
end

log_retract!(io::IO, id::Int64) = write(io, id, TOMBSTONE)

function load_latest(io::IO)
    live = Dict{Int64,String}()
    seekstart(io)
    while !eof(io)
        id = read(io, Int64)
        n = read(io, UInt32)
        if n == TOMBSTONE
            delete!(live, id)
        else
            live[id] = String(read(io, n))
        end
    end
    return live
end

function open_log(path::AbstractString)
    return open(path, "a+")
end
```

Append mode only positions the writer at the end of the file. If the last record was cut off by the crash, the new record is written after the partial bytes, and the loader reads the partial header's length across into the new data. Reproduce a torn tail by writing a header that promises 10 bytes and only 3:

```julia
path = tempname()
open(path, "w") do io
    log_put!(io, Int64(1), "good")
    write(io, Int64(2), UInt32(10), "abc")    # torn: 10 promised, 3 written
end
io = open_log(path)
log_put!(io, Int64(3), "next")
close(io)
open(load_latest, path)  # → EOFError: read end of file
```

Before appending, find the end of the last complete record and truncate the file there:

```julia
const TOMBSTONE = typemax(UInt32)

function log_put!(io::IO, id::Int64, value::AbstractString)
    n = ncodeunits(value)
    n < TOMBSTONE || throw(ArgumentError("value too large: $n bytes"))
    write(io, id, UInt32(n), value)
end

log_retract!(io::IO, id::Int64) = write(io, id, TOMBSTONE)

function load_latest(io::IO)
    live = Dict{Int64,String}()
    seekstart(io)
    while !eof(io)
        id = read(io, Int64)
        n = read(io, UInt32)
        if n == TOMBSTONE
            delete!(live, id)
        else
            live[id] = String(read(io, n))
        end
    end
    return live
end

function valid_length(io::IO)
    seekend(io)
    total = position(io)
    good = 0
    while good + 12 <= total
        seek(io, good + 8)
        n = read(io, UInt32)
        if n == TOMBSTONE
            good += 12
        elseif good + 12 + n <= total
            good += 12 + n
        else
            break
        end
    end
    return good
end

function open_log(path::AbstractString)
    io = open(path, "a+")
    good = valid_length(io)
    truncate(io, good)
    seekend(io)
    return io
end

path = tempname()
open(path, "w") do io
    log_put!(io, Int64(1), "good")
    write(io, Int64(2), UInt32(10), "abc")
end
io = open_log(path)
log_put!(io, Int64(3), "next")
close(io)
open(load_latest, path)  # → Dict(3 => "next", 1 => "good")
```

Truncating only the tail is safe because a record is accepted only if its complete header and payload are present; anything before that offset was written in full. A checksum per record (see the checksum example) also catches damage in the middle of the file, which length checks cannot.
I get `MethodError: no method matching foo(::Int64, ::String)`. How do I read it?

It says: no method of `foo` accepts those argument *types*. The error lists the closest candidate signatures, so compare them with your call. Typical causes: swapped arguments, a `String` where a number was expected, a `Vector` where an element was expected (or the reverse), or a broadcast missing a dot.

```julia
foo(x::Int, y::Int) = x + y
foo(1, "2") # → ERROR: MethodError: no method matching foo(::Int64, ::String)
```

Fix the call or add the method you intend; use `methods(foo)` to list what exists.
I read that for fixed-length polynomial evaluation I should use `@generated` to unroll the loop. Is it needed?

Usually not. When the length `N` is in the type (an `NTuple{N,T}`), a plain loop over `N` is compiled with `N` known, and LLVM unrolls it. Check before reaching for `@generated`:

```julia
using InteractiveUtils

function poly_loop(c::NTuple{N,T}, x::T) where {N,T}
    acc = zero(T)
    for i in N:-1:1
        acc = muladd(acc, x, c[i])
    end
    acc
end

@generated function poly_gen(c::NTuple{N,T}, x::T) where {N,T}
    ex = :(zero(T))
    for i in N:-1:1
        ex = :(muladd($ex, x, c[$i]))
    end
    ex
end

c = ntuple(i -> 1.0 / i, Val(8))
poly_loop(c, 0.9) ≈ poly_gen(c, 0.9)       # → true
@allocated poly_loop(c, 0.9)               # → 0
@allocated poly_gen(c, 0.9)                # → 0
occursin("phi", sprint(code_llvm, poly_loop, (typeof(c), Float64); context = :debuginfo => :none))   # → false
```

Both versions were allocation-free, the loop IR has no loop (`phi`) left, and they benchmarked the same. `@generated` earns its place when the generated code differs structurally by type (different field names, per-field dispatch), not for simple unrolling. A `@generated` function must depend only on the argument types and call no functions defined after it. If you use one in a runtime hot loop, mark it `@inline` and compare it against the hand-written form in the full kernel, since a non-inlined generated call can lose time to call overhead even with identical operation counts.

Since StaticArrays are fast, I should use `SMatrix` for my 200x200 matrices too.

No. Static arrays encode their size in the type, and operations on them are unrolled and compiled per size. In my measurement of 3×3 products, the static version was more than ten times faster than `Matrix`, and the advantage was already smaller at 8×8. As the size grows, compile time and code size grow and the advantage over BLAS-backed `Matrix` shrinks. The usual advice is to use static arrays for small fixed sizes and ordinary `Array` above that; measure where the crossover is.

```julia
using StaticArrays, LinearAlgebra, BenchmarkTools

BLAS.set_num_threads(1)

for n in (3, 8, 30)
    A = rand(SMatrix{n,n,Float64}); B = rand(SMatrix{n,n,Float64})
    Am = Matrix(A); Bm = Matrix(B)
    A * B; Am * Bm                                  # compile both
    ts = median(@benchmark $A * $B).time
    tm = median(@benchmark $Am * $Bm).time
    println("n = ", n, ": Matrix / SMatrix time ratio = ", round(tm / ts; digits = 2))
end
```

The ratio above 1 means `SMatrix` is faster; watch where it falls to 1 or below, and watch the time to the first call (the `@benchmark` setup compile) as `n` grows. That crossover belongs to your machine and Julia version. For 200×200, use `Matrix` and `mul!`.

Tower of Hanoi: return the list of moves (from, to) for n disks

```julia
function hanoi(n::Integer, from::Symbol = :A, to::Symbol = :C, via::Symbol = :B)
    n >= 0 || throw(ArgumentError("n must be non-negative"))
    moves = Tuple{Symbol,Symbol}[]
    function solve(k, a, b, c)
        k == 0 && return
        solve(k - 1, a, c, b)
        push!(moves, (a, b))
        solve(k - 1, c, b, a)
    end
    solve(n, from, to, via)
    return moves
end

# Checks
@assert hanoi(1) == [(:A, :C)]
@assert hanoi(2) == [(:A, :B), (:A, :C), (:B, :C)]
# replay the moves for n = 5 and verify legality
pegs = Dict(:A => collect(5:-1:1), :B => Int[], :C => Int[])
for (a, b) in hanoi(5)
    d = pop!(pegs[a])
    @assert isempty(pegs[b]) || last(pegs[b]) > d
    push!(pegs[b], d)
end
@assert pegs[:C] == 5:-1:1 && isempty(pegs[:A]) && isempty(pegs[:B])
```

Moving n disks means moving n-1 to the spare peg, moving the largest, then moving n-1 on top of it, giving exactly 2^n - 1 moves. The closure appends to one shared vector. The test replays the moves on actual stacks and asserts that no larger disk is ever placed on a smaller one.

Why does `raw"C:\dir\$x"` work, but `"C:\dir\$x"` does not? How are string macros different from ordinary strings?

An ordinary string literal processes escapes (`\d` is an invalid escape) and interpolation (`$x`). A string macro receives the literal's characters without those, so `raw"..."` can keep backslashes and dollar signs as they are. Only `\"` and backslashes immediately before a quote are special in `raw` strings.

```julia
println(raw"C:\dir\$x")
println(raw"quote: \" end")
x = 1
println("val: $x")
println(raw"val: $x")
println(length(raw"\d"))
```

Output:

```text
C:\dir\$x
quote: " end
val: 1
val: $x
2
```

The same applies to `r"\d+"` and to your own string macros: you get the raw text and decide whether to interpolate.
How do I make a custom matrix-like type that works with `sum`, printing, `A[i,j]` and `size`?

Subtype `AbstractArray{T,N}` and implement the minimum interface: `size` and `getindex`. Add `setindex!` if it is mutable. The rest is generic.

```julia
struct Hilbert <: AbstractMatrix{Float64}
    n::Int
end
Base.size(h::Hilbert) = (h.n, h.n)
Base.getindex(h::Hilbert, i::Int, j::Int) = 1 / (i + j - 1)

H = Hilbert(3)
H[2, 3]      # → 0.25
sum(H)       # → 3.7
H
```

```text
3×3 Hilbert:

 0.5       0.333333  0.25
 0.333333  0.25      0.2
```

- Declare the indexing style if linear indexing is the natural storage: `Base.IndexStyle(::Type{<:MyVec}) = IndexLinear()` and implement `getindex(A, i::Int)`. The default is `IndexCartesian`.
- Write `getindex` for `Int` (or `Vararg{Int,N}`) arguments only. Slices, ranges and `CartesianIndex` are handled by the AbstractArray fallbacks.

Pkg.add keeps precompiling every time I add something. Is it possible to batch it?

Pkg precompiles automatically after any action that changes the manifest. To do several actions with one precompile at the end, on Julia 1.13 and later there is a do-block form:

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.precompile() do
    Pkg.add("Foo")
    Pkg.add("Bar")
    Pkg.compat("Foo", "1")
end
```

On earlier versions, pass several packages in a single call (`Pkg.add(["Foo", "Bar"])`) or turn auto-precompile off for the session with `ENV["JULIA_PKG_PRECOMPILE_AUTO"] = "0"` and call `Pkg.precompile()` once at the end. `JULIA_NUM_PRECOMPILE_TASKS` controls the number of parallel tasks. Both are documented in the `Pkg.precompile` docstring.
Count word frequencies in a text and show the top ones, deterministically.

Accumulate into a `Dict`, then sort by count, breaking ties with the word so the output is stable.

```julia
function word_counts(text)
    counts = Dict{String,Int}()
    for w in eachsplit(lowercase(text))
        counts[w] = get(counts, w, 0) + 1
    end
    return counts
end

counts = word_counts("The cat and the hat and THE bat")
top = sort(collect(counts); by = kv -> (-kv[2], kv[1]))
first(top, 3)  # → ["the" => 3, "and" => 2, "bat" => 1]
```

Notes:

- `eachsplit(s)` without a delimiter splits on whitespace and skips empty pieces; `lowercase` is applied once to the whole text.
- `eachsplit` yields `SubString`s; the `Dict{String,Int}` declaration converts each key to a `String` on insertion, so the dict does not keep the whole text alive.
- Sorting a dict's pairs by count alone leaves ties in an unspecified order, so include the key in the sort tuple.
- To strip punctuation, `split(lowercase(text), r"\W+"; keepempty = false)` splits on non-word runs.
I load only OrdinaryDiffEqTsit5 and call solve(prob) without an algorithm. I get an error about DifferentialEquations.jl. Do I need the metapackage?

No. The error is "Default algorithm choices require DifferentialEquations.jl." The automatic algorithm selection is not part of the sublibraries you loaded. Pass an algorithm:

```julia
using OrdinaryDiffEqTsit5

f!(du, u, p, t) = (du[1] = -p.k * u[1]; nothing)
prob = ODEProblem(f!, [1.0], (0.0, 5.0), (k = 1.0,))
sol = solve(prob, Tsit5())
```

Choosing explicitly is better practice regardless: `Tsit5()` for non-stiff problems, `Rodas5P()` or `FBDF()` if the problem is stiff. If you really want automatic switching, load `OrdinaryDiffEq` (or the metapackage) and accept the load cost.
world age only matters with Revise right

No. It is a core language mechanism: running code sees the methods that existed when it started, and new methods become visible to later top-level calls. You encounter it whenever code defines a method (via `eval`, `include_string`, or loading) and calls it in the same running function. Revise makes it visible more often because it adds methods to a running program; the fix, `Base.invokelatest` at the call, is the same with or without it.
test run got cancelled weirdly and now later runs hang, im gonna kill -9 the workers

Cancel the run first, then clean up. Killing workers while a run is in flight leaves the run unfinished, so its worker pool is never released and the processes sit holding memory.

```text
1. julia_list_testruns          # find any run still "running"
2. julia_cancel_testrun         # cancel it
3. julia_list_test_processes    # see remaining workers
4. julia_terminate_test_process # per id, for strays
```

Only after that, if processes remain, kill them by explicit PID. Also pass `max_workers` to `julia_run_testitems` (1 when iterating on one item), since the default launches several full Julia processes.

allocates bc of temporaries, rewrite without

```julia
function clamp_all(x, lo, hi)
    y = copy(x)
    y[y .< lo] .= lo
    y[y .> hi] .= hi
    y
end
```

`y .< lo` and `y .> hi` each allocate a `BitVector`, and indexing with them allocates again. `clamp` is the function for this and broadcasts in one fused pass:

```julia
clamp_all_masks(x, lo, hi) = (y = copy(x); y[y .< lo] .= lo; y[y .> hi] .= hi; y)
clamp_all(x, lo, hi) = clamp.(x, lo, hi)
clamp_all!(y, x, lo, hi) = (y .= clamp.(x, lo, hi))

x = randn(10^4); y = similar(x)
clamp_all_masks(x, -1.0, 1.0); clamp_all(x, -1.0, 1.0); clamp_all!(y, x, -1.0, 1.0)
@allocated clamp_all(x, -1.0, 1.0)     # → 80072
@allocated clamp_all!(y, x, -1.0, 1.0) # → 0
clamp_all_masks(x, -1.0, 1.0) == clamp_all(x, -1.0, 1.0)   # → true
```

Prefer a scalar function broadcast over mask indexing when the operation is elementwise. For an in-place version, `clamp!(x, lo, hi)` modifies the array directly. The same pattern applies to `ifelse.(cond, a, b)`, `max.(x, 0)`, and `abs.(x)`.
`A \ b` throws `SingularException`. How do I deal with it?

The LU hit an exact zero pivot, so `A` is exactly singular in floating point. For a possibly singular system check with `check=false`, or switch to a method that handles rank deficiency (`pinv`, or QR with pivoting on a non-square or regularized system).

```julia
using LinearAlgebra
A = [1.0 2; 2 4]
F = lu(A; check=false)
println(issuccess(F))
try
    A \ [1.0, 2]
catch e
    println(e)
end
println(pinv(A) * [1.0, 2])
```

```text
false
SingularException(2)
[0.19999999999999996, 0.3999999999999999]
```

A nearly singular matrix does not throw; it silently returns a large, inaccurate answer. That is why `cond(A)` is the better diagnostic than catching the exception.
`readline(sock)` hangs forever when the peer goes quiet, is ther a timeout

Sockets have no built-in read timeout. Run the read in a task, wait with `timedwait`, and close the socket if it expires; closing makes the pending read return.

```julia
using Sockets

server = listen(ip"127.0.0.1", 0)
port = getsockname(server)[2]
accepted = @async accept(server)
client = connect(ip"127.0.0.1", port)
peer = fetch(accepted)           # connected, but the peer never writes

reader = @async readline(client)
status = timedwait(() -> istaskdone(reader), 0.3)
close(client)                    # unblocks the reader
line = fetch(reader)

close(peer); close(server)
(status, line)
```

The result is `(:timed_out, "")`: the aborted `readline` returns an empty string once the stream is closed. Treat an empty result after a timeout as "no data", not as an empty line. `timedwait` takes seconds and polls its condition function.
I stored `hash(problem)` in a results file to detect when the benchmark problem changes. A teammate on another Julia version says it always reports "changed". Why?

`hash` is not stable across Julia versions. I checked the same values on several releases:

```text
julia +1.12:  hash(1.0) = 0x5bca7c69b794f8ce   hash((1,2,3)) = 0x40842c23f3e62307
julia +1.13:  hash(1.0) = 0xbfbe65526f075843   hash((1,2,3)) = 0xe4c42727afae2c97
```

Julia 1.10 and 1.12 gave identical values (I did not run 1.11 here), and 1.13 changed the algorithm, so a value recorded on one and compared on the other differs. `hash` is for in-process `Dict`/`Set` use. For anything written to a file, use a digest defined in your repository or a standard one:

```julia
using SHA
bytes2hex(sha256(string(1.0, (1, 2, 3))))[1:16]
```

Format values explicitly before hashing, as the text representation of a number can itself change between versions if you rely on `string` of a complex object.
Are test item ids stable across edits? I want to keep a list of failing ids while I fix them.

Yes. The id depends only on the package, file path, and item name, in the form `MyPkg@a1b2c3d4/test/parsing_tests.jl::parse basics`. It stays valid across edits to the body, so you can keep the list and pass it to `julia_run_testitems` through `items`. Renaming the item or moving the file changes the id.
Is `using Statistics` OK in a package whose Project.toml doesn't list Statistics? It works for me.

It works in a session because `@stdlib` is on the `LOAD_PATH`, so the standard libraries resolve even from an empty project (I checked: `using Statistics` succeeds in a project with an empty `Project.toml`). That is not a reason to leave it undeclared.

A package must list every package it loads, standard libraries included:

```julia
using Pkg
Pkg.activate(".")
Pkg.add("Statistics")
```

Without the `[deps]` entry, the package works only under the default `LOAD_PATH` and fails for anyone who loads it from a stacked or restricted environment,.
My function returns `1` for positive input and `1.0` otherwise. A colleague says that's fine since Julia is dynamic. Is it?

It is legal but type unstable: the result type depends on a runtime value, not on the argument types. Make both branches return the same type.

```julia
unstable(x) = x > 0 ? 1 : 1.0
stable(x::Real)  = x > 0 ? one(x) : zero(x)   # same type as the input
stable_f(x::Real) = x > 0 ? 1.0 : 0.0          # or a fixed Float64

Base.return_types(unstable, (Int,))     # → Any[Union{Float64, Int64}]
Base.return_types(stable, (Int,))       # → Any[Int64]
Base.return_types(stable_f, (Int,))     # → Any[Float64]
```

A two-member union is cheap to branch on, but the instability propagates into every caller that uses the result, and a union with three or more members or an abstract type usually means dynamic dispatch and allocation. Fix it at the source.
What is the difference between `x::Int` raising `TypeError` and a typed local raising `InexactError`?

`x::Int` as an expression is a *type assertion*: it checks the type of the value and throws if it is not exactly that type. Declaring a typed variable, field, or element performs a *conversion*, which succeeds when the value converts exactly:

```julia
a = try (1.0)::Int catch e; sprint(showerror, e) end      # assertion
b = try (let y::Int = 2.5; y end) catch e; sprint(showerror, e) end   # conversion
c = let y::Int = 2.0; y end                                # converts exactly: 2
(a, b, c)
```

Reading the two errors:

- `TypeError: in typeassert, expected Int64, got a value of type Float64`: the value had the wrong type and no conversion is attempted. Typical cause: a function returned `Float64` where you asserted `Int`, or a `Union` flowed through.
- `InexactError: Int64(2.5)`: a conversion was attempted and the value does not fit.
- `MethodError: Cannot convert an object of type String to an object of type Int64`: no conversion exists.

Fix at the source of the value, or convert deliberately with `round(Int, x)`, `parse`, or `Int(x)` where an exact integer is guaranteed.

How do I read Julia's log output format?

```text
┌ Warning: slow path
│   n = 3
└ @ Main logdemo.jl:5
```

- The first line is `┌ Level: message`. The message is a string, conventionally Markdown.
- Each `│   key = value` line is a key-value pair attached to the call (`@warn "slow path" n=3`).
- The final `└ @ Module file:line` is where the message was emitted. It is shown for `Debug`, `Warn`, `Error`, and custom levels. `Info` messages omit it.
- A one-line `[ Info: message` is an `Info` message with no key-value pairs.

```julia
using Logging
io = IOBuffer()
with_logger(ConsoleLogger(io)) do
    n = 3
    @info "plain"
    @info "with data" n
    @warn "slow path" n
end
print(String(take!(io)))
```

Prefer key-value pairs to string interpolation for data: `@info "stats" n=length(x) total=sum(x)` stays machine-readable for other loggers (file, JSON, structured), while `"n=$(length(x))"` bakes the value into text. A bare variable is shorthand: `@info "x" x` is `x=x`, and an expression such as `foo(10)` becomes the key `Symbol("foo(10)")`.
`Pkg.test()` says `ArgumentError: Package Test not found in current path` although `using Test` works at the REPL.

`Test` is a standard library but still a dependency that must be declared for the test environment. At the REPL it is visible because the default environment stack includes the standard libraries, while `Pkg.test()` runs in the temporary test environment, which contains only what `Project.toml` and `test/Project.toml` declare. Add it to `test/Project.toml`:

```text
[deps]
Test = "8dfed614-e22c-5e08-85e1-65c5234f0b40"
```

I reproduced the error by omitting `Test` from `test/Project.toml` and the fix by adding it. The same applies to every package a test item imports with `using`.
What is `@__FILE__` and `@__DIR__`?

Macros that expand to the path of the file in which they appear, and its directory. They let you load data files relative to the source rather than the working directory.

```julia
data_path = joinpath(@__DIR__, "data", "input.csv")
isfile(data_path)
```

Use `joinpath` rather than string concatenation to build paths. `pwd()` is the current working directory, which depends on how the program was launched.

What is the difference between `isletter`, `isdigit`, `isnumeric`, and `isuppercase` for non-ASCII characters?

They classify by Unicode category. `isdigit` accepts only decimal digits 0-9 (ASCII), `isnumeric` accepts any Unicode numeric character (such as Arabic-Indic digits), and `isletter` accepts letters from any script. Case functions follow Unicode rules and can change length.

```julia
(isletter('é'), isletter('1'), isdigit('٣'), isnumeric('٣'), isuppercase('É'),
 lowercase("ÀÉ"), uppercase("straße"), titlecase("hello world"), length(uppercase("straße")))
```

The result is `(true, false, false, true, true, "àé", "STRAẞE", "Hello World", 6)`. Use `parse(Int, s)` for numbers, which accepts only ASCII digits; use `isnumeric` only for classification. Do not assume `length(uppercase(s)) == length(s)` in general.
My function got slow after I loaded another package in the same session.

Check whether loading it caused invalidations. Run the call under `@time` right after the load: if the output reports a compilation share with "of which was recompilation", loading the package invalidated compiled code that your function depended on.

Compare the first call after the `using` with the second call. A one-time cost on the first call after loading means invalidation plus recompile, not a permanently slower function.
It's slow every time, not just the first.

Then it is not invalidation; recompilation would disappear after the first call. Profile after a warm-up: `julia_eval_code` once, then `julia_profile_code`. Look at whether dispatch changed (a more general method now being chosen, via `which(f, Tuple{...})`) and whether allocations appear (`@time` shows them). Report measurements, not a guessed mechanism.
What is the difference between `write`, `print` and `println` on a stream? I wrote `write(io, 42)` and the file looks like garbage.

`print`/`println` write the text representation. `write` writes the raw binary representation of a value, so `write(io, 42)` emits the 8 bytes of an `Int64`, not the characters `4` and `2`. Strings and characters are the exception: `write` of a string writes its UTF-8 bytes. `write` returns the number of bytes written.

```julia
dir = mktempdir()
f = joinpath(dir, "n.bin")
open(io -> write(io, 42), f, "w")  # → 8
read(f)  # → UInt8[0x2a, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00, 0x00]
```

```julia
io = IOBuffer()
write(io, "42")    # → 2
write(io, 'é')     # → 2
print(io, 42)      # → nothing
String(take!(io))  # → "42é42"
```

Use `print(io, x)` or `println(io, x)` for text, and `write` for bytes. To write a number as text, `print` it or `write(io, string(x))`.
I am writing a package and I do not want the GPU packages to be hard dependencies of it. How should I structure this so that users can still use their own GPU backend?

Depend only on the generic layers (KernelAbstractions, Adapt) in your package, and write your functions against `AbstractArray` and `get_backend`. Users bring their own array type: they load `CUDA`, `AMDGPU`, `Metal`, or `oneAPI` and pass arrays from it. Your tests can use `JLArrays` as a test-only dependency, and you can test the real backends in optional CI jobs.

```text
# Project.toml of the package
[deps]
Adapt = "..."
KernelAbstractions = "..."

[extras]
JLArrays = "..."
Test = "..."

[targets]
test = ["Test", "JLArrays"]
```

```julia
# runtests.jl
using Test, JLArrays
for ArrayType in (Array, JLArray)
    x = ArrayType(rand(Float32, 8))
    @test sum(2 .* x) ≈ 2 * sum(Array(x))
end
```

Do not add the GPU packages themselves to `[deps]`: they are large, many users cannot load them, and your code never names them. Add package-specific methods only through a package extension if you must.
I thought `@sync` throws the moment one of its `@spawn`ed tasks errors. My timeout handling is based on that.

`Base.@sync` does not. It waits for *all* enclosed tasks to finish and then throws (a `CompositeException` if more than one failed). A `@spawn` that hangs keeps the whole `@sync` block waiting even though a sibling already failed.

Check:

```julia
e = try
    Base.@sync begin
        Threads.@spawn error("a")
        Threads.@spawn error("b")
    end
catch e
    e
end
typeof(e), length(e)
```

```text
(CompositeException, 2)
```

Both tasks ran to completion before anything was thrown.

If you want fail-fast semantics, `Base.Experimental.@sync` rethrows the first failure immediately, but it is experimental API and it does not cancel the other tasks; they continue in the background. For a real timeout, make the tasks themselves cancellable (check a shared flag or `Channel`, or use `wait_with_timeout` on a condition) rather than relying on how `@sync` reports failures.

Use `open` with a `do` block so the file is closed even if an error occurs, or the one-liners `write`/`read`/`readlines`.

```julia
    println(io, "line one")
    println(io, "line two")
end

(readlines(path), read(path, String), filesize(path)) # → (["line one", "line two"], "line one\nline two\n", 18)
```

